of the House: I can advise the House that when the House resumes on Tuesday, 27 May

items.text: Can I ask the acting
Acting Leader of the House whether there is  any intention to progress the Veterans’

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I was hoping that he
would ask me about all my Treaty legislat ion. There is more on the Order Paper now
than there ever was under that party’s—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Budget 2014—Business Growth Agenda
1. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Finance : How
does Budget 2014 contribute to building a more productive and competitive economy
through the Government’s Business Growth Agenda?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : Budget 2014 contains a range of initi atives across the Business Growth
Agenda. As everyone now knows, we have ente red a period of signi ficant growth for
the New Zealand economy that is lifting j ob numbers and incomes. The challenge for
the Business Growth Agenda is to keep reducing some of the longer-term capacity
constraints in areas like sk ills and innovation, so that  the New Zealand economy can
continue to grow at a faster  rate than it has in the past, for an extended period. One
important area is building our  international markets. Budget 2014 provides funding of
$69 million over the next 4 years for New Ze aland Trade and Enterprise to boost its
presence in China, South America, and th e Middle East, and to lift the number of
companies it works with intensively from 500 to 700.
Simon O’Connor : How does Budget 2014 contribut e to lifting research and
innovation in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Budget continues this  Government’s long and
extensive initiatives in the research and development area. This Budget contains an
additional $58.6 million over 3 years for additional contestable science and innovation
funding, which will take the total annual Government investment to $1.5 billion by
2015-16. High-quality scientific re search is, of course, crit ical to increasing innovation
and economic growth. The Budget also contains  two tax measures to benefit businesses
investing in research and development. Loss-making start-up companies will be able to
cash out all or part of their tax losses from research and development expenditure, while
18246 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014
all businesses will be allowed tax deductibility for research and development black hole
expenditure, which is currently neither deducti ble nor able to be depreciated. These tax
changes will help us meet ou r goal of increasing business research and development to
1 percent of GDP.
Simon O’Connor: How does Budget 2014 contribute to lifting the skill levels of the
New Zealand workforce?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Budget contains additionally nearly $200 million of
initiatives over the next 4 years. Tuition subs idies for science, agriculture, and selected
health sciences will be lift ed, which comes on top of funding increases for engineering
and science in previous Budgets. Additional funding also means the Government will be
funding 10 centres of resear ch excellence from 2016-17, up from the six that were
recently selected through the competitive pro cess. The Government will also spend an
additional $20 million expanding the very su ccessful apprenticeship reboot programme
by an additional 6,000 places, bringing the number of places to 20,000.
Simon O’Connor : How is the Government’s su ccessful share offer programme
helping to pay for new infrastructure inve stment, as part of the Business Growth
Agenda?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government’s successful share offer programme raised
around $4.7 billion, which is being invested  in new priority public assets and
infrastructure, without taxpaye rs having to borrow this mone y from overseas lenders.
Budget 2014 allocated another $1 billion for these investments, which will be made
through the Future Investment Fund. That brin gs allocations from the fund so far to
almost $3 billion, leaving nearly $1.7 billi on in the fund for spending on more new
assets in the next two Budgets. Future Investment Fund allocations in this Budget
included $67 million for the new Grey Base Hospital on the West Coast, $172 million
for the upgrading and building of new school s, including the Pegasus Bay school in
North Canterbury, $75 million for Christchurch housing, $40 million for Crown
Irrigation Investments, and $30 million for the Hobsonville housing development. All of
these things would not have been possibl e unless we had had the programme of the
mixed-ownership model.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: If, as he claims, the economy will become more competitive and
productive, why is it that imports are forecast to grow far faster than exports for the next
4 years, increasing our external deficit to $16 billion by 2017?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the member needs to look at the progress that this
Government has already made, despit e various prognostications by certain
commentators, including Treasury. This year the balance of payments deficit is down to
about 3.5 percent of GDP and forecast to go lowe r. If the member thinks that it is as
good as it gets, well, it is a heck of a lot better than the 8 percent when he was in charge.
Climate Change—Economic Impact and Greenhouse Gas Emissions
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: Does
he stand by all his statements?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: Yes. He particularly stands by his st atement, which was originally made by
the Prime Minister, in fact, that Budget 2014 is a confident Budget for a confident
country.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his statemen t in this House on 14 May last
year that “It is important for New Zealand … that it is regarded as a good credit risk.”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: That sounds like a very good stat ement that the Minister of
Finance would make.
22 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18247

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given his acknowledgment that a good credit rating is
important for New Zealand, is he concerned by the warning from Standard and Poor’s
last week that New Zealand’s sovereign credit rating is at risk due to climate change?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and the reason for that is that the Government’s books,
which are the primary concern of the Stan dard and Poor’s organisation, are moving
positively into the black. We will have the opportunity to repay debt, and we will reduce
our debt as a percentage of  GDP to 20 percent by 2019-20, on schedule. In relation to
any concerns about climate change, this Government is undertaking a very strong
programme to mitigate the effects of climat e change and become a less carbon-intense
economy over time, while not jeopardising our ability to raise moneys and pay off debt.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he aware that Moritz Kraem er, Standard and Poor’s chief
sovereign risk analyst, has identified clim ate change as one of the century’s two
defining macroeconomic trends that are lik ely to put downward pr essure on countries’
sovereign credit ratings?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: That would depend on how the countries respond to those
risks. Countries always have risks. If the member wants to go and look at some of the
more recent data, he will see that New Z ealand’s carbon intensity is continuing to
decline. In other words, the amount of carbon we produce as our economy grows is
reducing as a percentage of GDP. That is a good thing and su ggests that we are doing a
good job as a country in mitigating the risk identified.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given the Minister’s answer, can we assume that he is not
aware that Standard and Poo r’s has listed New Zealand’s credit rating as particularly
vulnerable to climate change, because of the proportion of our population living on the
coast and because of agriculture’s role in our economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The answer to the first part of his question is that, no, we
cannot assume that. Secondly, if the member  is suggesting that New Zealand knock the
agricultural economy on the head  to meet the needs of clim ate change, I imagine that
Standard and Poor’s would have a view of that and it would not be positive.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Will he now finally acknowledge the seriousness of climate
change for New Zealand when not only are the world’s leading climate scientists saying
that our environment and our communities are at risk but one of the world’s largest
rating agencies is also saying that our credit rating could suffer as a result of climate
change?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject the implicit arrogance in the member’s question that
the Government does not understand the import ance of the risks of climate change.
Actually, this Government is focused on mee ting all the fiscal risks that New Zealand
faces, and if he goes and has a look at the data, he will see the reducing intensity of New
Zealand’s carbon emissions as a percentage  of our GDP. That is  something to be
celebrated and I am confident it will continue under this Government.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has the Minister gone to look at the data—for example, the
Ministry for the Environment’s most recent data—which shows that the projections for
New Zealand’s net emissions are that they will increase by 50 percent over the next
decade under current settings of this Govern ment, and does he believe that that is a
responsible projection for New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: We discussed in the prev ious question the issue of
projections. What I can tell the member is that what has occurred under this
Government is a decreasing intensity of carbon emissions as our economy grows. The
member may not like to know that, but that  is true. We also have an increasing
percentage of, for example, our electric ity generation in renewables, and this
Government’s record on the environment— again, not something the Greens want to
talk about—is very good and compares favourably with the previous Government.
18248 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: In light of official reports fr om his Government showing a big
increase in projected emissions ahead, will he  take advice as to what should be the
response of the Government to the Standard  and Poor’s report, which has identified
New Zealand as vulnerable due to the number of  New Zealanders likely to be impacted
by sea level rise and due to the large cont ribution agriculture ma kes to our economy,
and that agriculture is particularly vulnerable to climate change?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, this Government takes advice on those sorts of risks
every day and we have, for example, in  the Business Growth Agenda, a group of
Ministers in the natural res ources area who grapple with these issues on an ongoing
basis and actually make decisions every da y that mitigate those risks, and we will
continue to do so. But if the member is s uggesting, as I believe he may be, that we
quickly shut down the agricultural industry so as  to avoid that risk, I suspect that is not
something we will agree about.
Economy—Regional Development, Timber Processing Industry, and
Wage Growth
3. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour) to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : Does he agree with the Mayor of Clutha district
that the loss of the 180 jobs in the wood pr ocessing industry is a “hammer blow” to the
region?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): No. I understand the mayor being con cerned at the loss of an employer
in his district, but, despite the tendency of a number of people to talk down the Otago
economy, the region is doing very well. The latest household labour force survey shows
a net increase in Otago of 8,000 jobs in th e last year—8,000 jobs in the last year.
Unemployment in the Otago region is one of  the lowest in New Zealand, at 4.6 percent
compared with the national average of 6 percent. The ANZ Regional Trends report
released on Tuesday said that Otago has the highest level of business confidence and
one of the fastest economic gr owth rates in the whole of New Zealand. That is not the
Opposition’s spin but actually what is happening under this Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Has he not read the ANZ Regional Trends report, which, for the
adjacent province of Southland, shows that “S outhland recorded the largest decrease in
employment, dropping 4.0 percent in the quarter to hit a 10-year low. The region’s
unemployment rate deteriorated, hitting a 10-y ear high …”, or is that just because its
local MPs are Bill English and Eric Roy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would have thought that Mr Parker, as a former resident
of the Otago region, would know that the Clutha district is  in the Otago region and not
in the Southland region, but, unfortunately, Mr  Parker is not aware of that, which is
probably why he was never able to hold on to the seat of Otago—because he never even
went there.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why has he refused to set any targets for regional development
growth in his department’s annual statement of intent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Firstly, again, the member ma y not be aware, but I would
have thought he has been around long enough to  know that that is developed by the
agency, not by the Minister. The good news is that every region in the New Zealand
economy is growing, and every region, if he  looks at the ANZ Regional Trends, is
growing strongly. That is the reality. Mr  Parker may obsess about writing down a
number, but the real question, and where the rubber meets the road, is job growth and
GDP growth in the regions. The reality is that we are seeing in Otago very strong
growth, which is very good for that region, and I am very pleased for it. I think it is
probably time the Opposition declared an Otago crisis.
22 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18249

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why has his Government de serted the wood-processing
industry nationwide, with net job losse s of around 3,000 since 2008, when those job
losses show that the sector so seriously needs an economic upgrade?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It “so seriously needs an  economic upgrade” that an
investor went out 2 weeks ago and spent a billion dollars purchasing assets in the
forestry processing industry. Of course, they see a strong future in that industry, and it is
ridiculous for the member to suggest that that is otherwis e. Yes, individual companies
have difficulties from time to time, and th e company that was th e subject of this
question has had financial difficulties for some time. Mr Parker may be of the view that
the Government should rescue every investor  from the challenges that they may or may
not operate in, but this Government knows that the job is ac tually encouraging
investment across New Zealand industries and—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question is now answered.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why is real wage growth forecast to average less than 1
percent—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, rubbish.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: —for the next 3 years, accord ing to his own Budget—it is not
rubbish—which is lower than increases in GDP per capita, and is this because under
National the benefits of economic growth can  never be expected to flow through to
working New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member is absolutely wrong. The way you build
incomes for New Zealand families is to en courage investment and growth across New
Zealand. That is what this G overnment is doing. We can se e that in the growth figures,
in the export figures, and in the employment figures. We can see it  in the balance of
payment figures. We can see it in New Zeala nd’s net international liability figures. We
can see it across every measure of the Ne w Zealand economy. The Opposition may not
like it, but actually we are growing incomes for Kiwi families.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: What specific actions has he pla nned to increase the economic value
from the volume of the timber and wood-pr ocessing industry in Otago and Southland,
given that his own department says growth in the region “will depend on the application
of capital and technology to natural sources.”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: There is a range of things. I know the member has not read
it, but we have 350 serious initiatives in the Business Growth Agenda. For example, one
growing—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: They’re not working.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: They are working—4.6 percent growth in Otago. Oh yes,
they are working. And the reality is that we have—

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. With respect, my question was
regarding specific actions his department would undertake for a specific industry—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member asked what sp ecific actions, and the Minister
rose to his feet and said th ere were 350 of them and talk ed about the Business Growth
Agenda and its application. [ Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. On this occasion the
Minister has addressed the question.
Budget 2014—Child Health Services
4. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister of Health : What investment is the
Government making in Budget 2014 to improve health outcomes for children?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government is investing $90
million over 3 years from 1 July 2015 so prim ary school - aged children can go to the
doctor for free at any time of the day or night and get their prescriptions for free as well.
This builds on the success of the free general practitioners visits and prescriptions for
18250 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014
children under 6, including fr ee after-hours visits. Thanks to our prudent management
of the health budget, we can now extend this policy to all children under 13, and that is
what careful financial management of the country’s finances can deliver for Kiwi
families.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What recent reports has he received on the new policy to provide free
general practitioners visits and prescriptions for under-13s?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: This policy has been widely welcomed in the health sector,
including by the Medical Association, the Pa ediatric Society, the College of General
Practitioners, and the New Zealander of the Year, Kait āia general practitioner Lance
O’Sullivan. I have also seen a report th at somewhat begrudgingly described the
extension of free general practitioners visits and prescriptions as an “attractive policy”.
That was from the Leader of the Opposition, David Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: What will the Government do to improve the effectiveness of the
rheumatic fever campaign, given that a recent  study has shown that fewer than one in
three children prescribed antibiotics for rheumatic fever had taken the full course?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government is investing $20 million in expanding the
rheumatic fever programme in this year’s B udget. One of the items that that money will
be invested in is improving adherence and looking at new and innovative ways that we
can encourage that.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What other initiatives announced in the Budget will support the good
health of New Zealand children?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: It is more good news for Kiwi families in this year’s Budget.
Very positive announcements—the $20 million for the Rheumatic Fever Prevention
Programme extension, which I talked about earlier; $6.3 million to provide bilateral
cochlear implants for children; and $40 million for the new Healthy Families NZ anti-
obesity programme, to help encourage mo re New Zealanders to eat healthier and
exercise more.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: What is the Ministry of Health doing to ensure that general
practitioners consistently prescribe adequa te courses of antibiotics for rheumatic
fever—for example, 10 days, rather than a lesser amount, which is sometimes the case?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Ministry of Health is working very actively with the
general practice community in order to improve  services for kids who present with sore
throats. One of the things we are funding out of this $5 million a year—$20 million over
4 years—in this year’s  Budget is the expansio n of drop-in sore thro at clinics. Most of
these are based in general practice. They are free, which is designed to encourage
people to present and then get the various antibiotics and medica tions that might be
required after that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary question, the Hon Annette King.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: A blast from the past.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Sit down, sonny.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is the sort of disorder  that is created by an interjection
from my right-hand side, and it will cease.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of the New Zealand Me dical Association saying that it
needs more detail of the policy, how many c onsultations per child per year, on average,
did he base his announcement of $30 million a year to pay ge neral practitioners for free
doctors visits for children under 13 years of age?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As the member knows, we will be entering negotiations with
general practice on that, so that informati on would be commercially sensitive at this
stage. But what I have got to  tell that member is that I do not know why she is so
opposed to this policy, because when I was meeting with general practitioners in her
electorate at lunchtime, they were very supportive.
22 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18251
GCSB—2011 Briefings and Appointment of Director
5. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central) to the Prime Minister:
Was a staff member from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet present at the
briefing on Operation Debut held on 14 Dece mber 2011; if so, was that same person
present at his meeting with Simon Murdoch and Ian Fletcher on the 12 th of December
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Prime Minister
items.text: I am advised that the answer to the first part of the question is no; it
then follows that the answer to the second part of the question is also no.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that the Government paid the cost for Ian Fletcher to
come to New Zealand for the meeting on 12 December?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I do not have that particular piece of information to hand
this afternoon.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek the leave of the Hous e to table a screenshot of a
Queensland Department of State travel  expense form, which shows a $1,060
contribution from the New Zealand Government to Ian Fletcher’s travel.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is this something that has been freely broadcast to all New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He doesn’t know about it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not the question I asked. Is this something that has
been screened on public TV to all New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It has.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Then that information is freely available.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of the fact that th e New Zealand Government did pay
$1,060 to Ian Fletcher for him to come to  New Zealand on 12 December, why did the
Prime Minister say yesterday that Ian Fletcher “happened to be in New Zealand” for the
meeting?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I appreciate Perry Mason’s efforts in this regard. What I
can tell the member—

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: “CSI Karori”.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —“CSI Karori”—is that the 12 December 2011 meeting
occurred between the Prime Minister, Mr Ferguson, and Mr Murdoch, the then Acting
Director of the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB).

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You’re struggling.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not struggling at all,  thank you very much. That
information is well known.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. In Mr Joyce’s attempts to
answer that question, he did not address the question I asked, which was about why the
Prime Minister yesterday said—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is making a reasonable point. There was too
much noise throughout the question and the answer. I invite the member to ask the
question again.

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: Have another go, Grissom.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: We will come to you, too.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just ask the question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of the fact that th e New Zealand Government did pay
$1,060 for Ian Fletcher to come to New Z ealand on 12 December, why did the Prime
Minister say yesterday that Ian Fletcher “happened to be in New Zealand” for the
meeting?
18252 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Because he did happen to be in New Zealand for the
meeting.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How can any of the Prime Minister ’s claims about Ian Fletcher’s
appointment be taken with any credibility when  he claimed in this House that his only
role in appointing Ian Fletcher was to accep t the recommendation of  the State Services
Commissioner, when, in fact, he  organised a meeting with Ia n Fletcher 3 days after he
approved the appointment panel for the GCSB job, he personally called Ian Fletcher and
told him to contact a member of the appoint ment panel, and Ian Fl etcher was the only
person interviewed for the job? Is it not about time that he stopped telling lies to New
Zealanders—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! That question is out of order.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Every member has a right to raise a point of order, and it
will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: My understanding of the precedent of the use of the word
“liar” is that in the past it has always been with regard to statements in the House. There
was not a suggestion that the statement that the Prime Minister made was one made in
the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I need no more assistance. Th at sort of question will lead to
disorder in this House, and on that basis it was ruled out of—[Interruption] Order! If the
member wants to add to his record of leaving the House by talking when I am talking to
a point of order, we will ensure that that happens.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Again, this is a point of order. It will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I draw your attention to the answers that Mr Joyce gave on behalf
of the Prime Minister, which deliberately avoided answering the question. We had to
force him to answer another question. All of his answers were, in fact, out of order.
They all began with an insult to me as a questioner. So if you are looking for where
disorder starts in the House, it starts with Mr Joyce—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! In my opinion the Minister addressed every question apart
from one. I gave the member the opportunity to then ask that question again, to which,
to my satisfaction, the Minister then addressed that question.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If it is a relitigation of this matter, I will take that very seriously.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: While Grant Robertson made hi s point of order, Mr Joyce
interjected five times and was not reprimanded.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I called for silence throughout that point of order. If the Hon
Steven Joyce did interject through that point of order, then I now require him to leave

whether he did interject.

Budget 2014—Schools
6. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister of Education : How will
Budget 2014 continue to support schools?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Budget 2014 continues to support
schools through new investments, big and small. Over and above the $359 million
flagship initiative investing in teachers and school leaders, we are investing a further
$284 million into building new schools and cl assrooms, on top of the $1.1 billion into
Greater Christchurch. Operational grants wi ll be increased by a further 2 percent at a
22 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18253
cost of $85 million, and $4.7 million is being invested for children with high health
needs to safely attend school, learn, and achieve.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How do operational grants support schools to be successful?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Operational grants are about 20 percent of total
Government funding to schools. The operational grants support schools to be successful
by giving them choice and flexibility in how  they deliver the cu rriculum programme
they have decided upon together with their parent communities. This means that we will
be spending $1.23 billion on school operation al grants alone over the next year to
support schools like Ongaonga from the central  Hawke’s Bay, which is in the gallery
today.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How is it fair that the Budget gives additional funding for charter
schools, meaning that for at least one charter school its per student funding will be more
than $40,000 a student, whereas State schools have to struggle by with an increase that
barely meets the cost of inflation?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Partnership schools, of whic h there are five out of over
2,500 schools, are receiving funding that amount s to two-tenths of 0.1 percent of the
$10 billion.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How is it fair?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: How it is fair is because our system has been failing a
certain cohort of our population for many a long year. If we continue to do all the same
things we have always done, we will get th e same results we have always got. This
Government is not prepared to accept that. It wants five out of five children being
successful.
Health and Safety, Workplace—Bullying, Discrimination, and Harassment
7. BRENDAN HORAN (Independent) to the Minister of Labour: What measures
is the Government taking to address th e problems of bullying, discrimination, and
harassment occurring in New Zealand workplaces?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Bullying in the workplace is
unacceptable. This difficult issue can adversel y affect people’s personal health and can
seriously impact business productivity. Our em ployment health and safety law provides
explicit protection for employees from bullying, discrimination, and harassment.
Additionally, in February this year WorkSa fe New Zealand, in conjunction with the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employ ment, issued best-practice guidelines on
workplace bullying. The guidelines seek to support those involved in responding to
situations before they get out of hand.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Would those guidelines provide protections to ensure that a
member of Parliament or a party leader cannot bully—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a question to the Minister of Labour. Further
supplementary questions that the member asks must relate to a ministerial responsibility
of the Minister as Minister of Labour. I invite him to ask his question.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. I am referring to workplace
bullying.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will listen very carefully to the question, but the member is at risk.
If I consider he is asking a question that does not have direct ministerial responsibility, I
have two courses of action: either to leave it to the Minister to answer it that way or I
have the option to rule it out of order.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Would those guidelines provide protections to ensure that a
member of Parliament or a party leader cannot bully or intimidate a Parliamentary
18254 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014
Service employee into conducting unlawful activities—for example, accessing the
emails of another member without that member’s permission?

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I believ e this question is out
of order. I draw your attention to Standing Order 375(b), relating to the responsibility of
the Minister, and also to Standing Orders 377(1)(a) and 377(1)(c), which state,
respectively, that statements given as fact must be able to be authenticated, and that
statements must not contain discreditable references to any member of Parliament.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On the occasion I am going to invite  the Minister to answer it. He
needs to answer it very carefully in line with his ministerial responsibility.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is difficult to answer such a question in the abstract, and
I do not comment, of course, on specific cases. I suspect the matter the member refers
to, if it were made out, is one for the Parliamentary Service.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Would those guidelines mean that an employee who made a
complaint to her employer about abusive emails and text messages from her boss should
be able to respond to that person’s public de nials without fear of legal action; if not,
why not?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there is minister ial responsibility —the Hon Simon
Bridges.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Referring back again to
Standing Order 375(b) and the matters of ad ministration for which the Minister is
responsible, I believe that the Minister, as th e Minister of Labour, is one of a number of
Ministers responsible for the Ministry of  Business, Innovation and Employment, and,
therefore, WorkSafe New Zeal and, but he is not specifically  solely responsible, and the
question should have been directed to a Mini ster in his or her capacity as the Minister
responsible for the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not accept that part. We allowed the first question through
marginally on the question around guidelines. This is a further explanation or request
for an explanation from the Minister about those guidelines. The question stands.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Effectively, my answer to the earlier supplementary
question still stands. I am sure that Parlia mentary Service is aware of best-practice
guidelines on bullying and is incorporating them as appropriate. As a general statement
of principle, bullying is unacceptable no matter where or when it occurs.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Does the Minister believe that an employee locked out of her
office by her boss should be allowed to ch allenge that boss’s publ ic denials and the
denials of his colleagues without fear of legal action?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is an opinion question, and again, in so far as there is
ministerial responsibility, I call the Hon Simon Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I think that is a matter of opinion and, indeed, one that
requires a legal opinion. I will  repeat, really, all that I have said. Bullying is
unacceptable no matter where or when it occurs.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary question—Jacinda Ardern. [ Interruption] Oh,
sorry—Brendon Horan. It is actually not that easy a mistake to make but I still managed

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Would those guidelines mean that MPs might have to take
responsibility for their treatment of staff,  rather than hiding behind Parliamentary

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That question is definitely out of order. Any issues regarding

Police Resourcing—Funding and Alternative Approaches
8. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour) to the Minister of Police: Does she stand by her
statement in relation to Budget 2014 that “The Police’s core operating spending is being
maintained”?
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Justice) on behalf of the Minister of Police:
Yes.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Was the Police Association correct when it stated that “police are
receiving around $40 million less to do the job than they sp ent last year. We are no
longer frozen, we are going backwards,”; if  not, what is the di fference in output
expenses between the two Budgets?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The association is correct that there is $40 million, which
was a result of one-off funding delivered by th e Government for certain things. Those
matters that it was funded for were from the Justice Sector Fund to enable a
restructuring of human resources and fina nce; the retention of a road policing
underspend, which helped deliver the lowest ro ad toll in 60 years; the completion of the
police’s deployment to the Solomon Isla nds; and one-off funding for the police to
implement the Criminal Procedure Act. Th e core operating spending is actually being
maintained at $1.46 billion, and there has b een no cut at all in the core operating
spending or funding.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Will she adopt the New Zealand First policy of minimum double
staffing of patrol cars at night, which will see a significant reduction in assaults on our
police, or do flat and reducing Budgets prevent this?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, I do not believe that the Minister would be
adopting that, because that would be an ope rational matter for police, but I can tell the
member—and I hope this will assist—that wh en this has previously been looked at
under a previous Minister, it was rejected by the police for very sound reasons. It would
have meant, in fact, that there would be a lot of police unable to service areas because of
shift requirements, holiday requirements, and others.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Was the extra funding from the Justice Sector Fund that the
Minister referred to, which is  to pay for basic human resources, proof that she has
significantly underfunded the police in 2013 and has done so again?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I am sorry, but the member has misheard. I said that the
funding from the Justice Sector Fund was to enable a restructure of human resources
and finance. That is not actually basic human resources work.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: What additional resources has this Government provided to police
to fight crime and keep our communities safer?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: This Government has f unded police to recruit an
additional 600 police officers, and we have rolled out sm artphones and tablets to all
front-line officers. This new technology ha s freed police up from paperwork, and got
them out on to the street delivering the equivalent of 354 additional officers—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: —354 additional officers. We have also implemented a
new policing model, which is focused on preventing crime rather than simply reacting
to it, and the results speak for themselves. Over the last 4 years crime has fallen by over
20 percent, and the recorded crime rate is th e lowest that it has been in a generation.
Under the previous Government, crime was increasing.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she believe that responding to crime quickly, good resolution
rates, and crime prevention have a role to pl ay in keeping crime down; if so, how does
Budget 2014 support those initiatives?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, clearly they do.
18256 Questions for Oral Answer 22 May 2014

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Can she confirm that the police have cut back on the amount of
live ammunition allocated to each police officer ’s annual firearms training to no more
than 30 rounds per officer per year because of cost cutting due to flat Budgets, and does
she believe this level will provide police with  an adequate degree of competency in the
use of firearms?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I really would not know about that.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: In light of her previous answer , can she confirm that this Budget
includes a $3.5 million cut to general crime prevention, a $7 million cut to
investigations, a $7 million cut to primar y response, and a $10 million cut to road
policing, and is she seriously telling the public that it can expect the same level of
service from the police with cuts like that?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: As I have already said to the member, this Government is
about results. The police have shown th at by using technology, and by having a
Minister who backs the police and does not consistently deride them—as that member
would, should she ever have  the opportunity—the police can in fact produce results,
which means that the crime rate itself is now down to the lowest it has been since 1978,
before that member was even born.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: In the wake of such significant  cuts to the police budget and the
risk of increasing operational failures that wi ll affect the public, is she content that in
contrast to that, the Diplomatic Protectio n Squad’s funding has increased by 63 percent
since she took office?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I am sure the member is aware that the way in which the
police allocate their funding is an operati onal decision for the Commissioner of Police,
and is not something undertaken by the Mini ster. That member shakes her head, but,
unfortunately, I am right and she is not.
Tourism Promotion—Funding, Impact, and Adventure Tourism Safety
9. JOANNE HAYES (National)  to the Minister of Tourism : What recent
investments has this Government made to grow the tourism sector in New Zealand?
Hon TODD McCLAY (Associat e Minister of Tourism)  on behalf of the Minister
of Tourism : Just this week we announced that  the Government’s Tourism Growth
Partnership is investing $3.84 million in six inno vative tourism projects that will create
jobs in New Zealand. This is in addi tion to the $23 million in co-funding for the
applicants, making a total of $26.84 million of new investment in the tourism industry.
The six projects are Rotorua’s Skyline Grav ity Park, Auckland Airport’s food and wine
cluster project, New Zealand Ski’s virtual guest services platform, The Orange Group’s
project to target Chinese visitors, the Ch ristchurch Adventure Park, and Bachcare’s
online holiday rental project. These projects represent a potential industry investment of
$6 for every $1 invested by the Government. This is a great return.

items.speaker: Joanne Hayes
items.text: When the Minister made this announcement at Trenz, New
Zealand’s largest tourism trade show, this week, what was the mood of the industry?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In as far as there is ministerial responsibility, the Hon Todd
McClay.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: The mood of the industry is purely a ministerial
responsibility. The industry is in good heart. This y ear 250 New Zealand tourism
businesses exhibited at Trenz and 250 buye rs from around the world attended. The
industry is benefiting from having a high- profile Minister who is promoting New
Zealand tourism around the world, and a Gove rnment that has invested heavily in
targeted markets. Recently, as Associat e Minister, I met with a number of key
representatives of the British travel industry in London. Many of them expressed a real
22 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 18257
sense of optimism in having New Zealand as  a tourism destination and lauded Tourism
New Zealand’s outstanding overseas promotional work.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A point of order has been called, so the normal rules apply.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would ju st like you to point out to
the Minister that he was answering on beha lf of the Minister of Tourism, and the
activities of the Associate Mi nister should not be taken into account in that answer,
unless he says “on behalf of the Minister, the Associate Minister  did something”. He
has got the wrong person.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the point that the member is making. Ministers should
recall that when they are answ ering on behalf of a Minister, they need to initiate their
answer with that comment. But I am sure, on my interpretation of that answer, he was
actually interpreting the actions of the Mini ster, rather than those of the Associate
Minister.

items.speaker: Joanne Hayes
items.text: When the Minister was at Tr enz last year, he committed an
additional $158 million towards tourism over th e next 4 years. What progress is he
seeing?

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: We are seeing great progress. There were 2.78 million
visitor arrivals in New Zealand in the year to April 2014, which is 6 percent higher than
in 2013. This includes growth from Australi a of 5.5 percent; from Asia, which is up by
8.3 percent; from Europe, which is up by 6.8 pe rcent; and from the Americas, which is
up by 8.8 percent. This Government’s support for a far more proactive and coordinated
tourism strategy is really starting to pay dividends. In the most recent international
visitor survey, the total visitor spend in Ne w Zealand was up by 9 percent, to almost $7
billion. A recent New Zealand Institute of Economic Research report showed that
within five of our major tourism markets, the promotion of New Zealand was found to
have had considerable impact on the choi ce of people—more good news for the New
Zealand tourism sector.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Has he not broken his promise that he made to grieving families to
clean up safety in the adventure tourism indus try when progress on the safety audits has
stalled because of his Government’s failure to properly resource safety audit providers?

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: No, that is not correct. The Prime Minister and Ministers
have worked very hard in this area. Indeed, the Government is committed to assisting
the adventure activities sector to meet its  obligation and deadlin e of 1 November to
register under the Health and Safety in  Employment Regulations. Approximately 460
adventure tourism activity operators are subject to these regulations, and WorkSafe New
Zealand, which administers the regulations, has developed solutions to help these
operators meet this deadline of 1 November.

Canterbury, Recovery—Protection of Migrant Workers
12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister of Immigration : What
recent announcements has he made to help combat the exploitation of migrant workers
helping on the Canterbury rebuild?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yesterday the
Minister of Labour, Simon Bridges, and I announced more than $7 million over the next
4 years from Budget 2014 to boost the number of labour inspectors  and immigration
officers dealing with the Canterbury rebu ild. The money will be used to fund an
additional six labour inspectors and seven immigration staff, including three compliance
officers and two investigators. This will result in much greater capacity to educate
about, to prevent, and then to prosecute exploitative practices.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Why is this extra funding necessary at this time?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: The Canterbury rebuild is one of the
Government’s top priorities, and as the rebu ild gathers momentum it is very important
that we provide the tools needed to stamp out unlawful practices and provide assurances
that maintain our international reputation. These extra inspectors augment the law
changes announced last year that in troduced tough new penalties for migrant
exploitation by employers, but I note with interest that the Labour Party and the Greens
have said that they will vote against the bill currently before the House that would
implement these changes.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: How will this announcement help Filipino migrants Carlos Claveron
and Emmanuel Francisco, who paid $15,000 to an  immigration adviser in return for a
job paying $18 an hour, but then had their pa y cut by $3 a hour when they arrived in
New Zealand, yet months later the labour inspector is telli ng them there is nothing they
can do?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: It will help people like those Filipino workers in
a number of ways. Firstly, it will help by  ensuring that they have appropriate
information—both them and their employers—on what is appropriate practice in New
Zealand, and that where employers fall belo w that standard th ere are appropriate
avenues of inquiry, including the actions that the member has taken. I also imagine that
there would be a part to play for trade unions in supporting workers like them through
that process, and I am quite sure that the member would be referring workers to them.
Debate resumed from 21 May on the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: What a fantastic Budget we have
had. What a fantastic Budget.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: How would you know? You weren’t here. You were on leave.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I loved being here last Thursday to be here for the
Budget, but Mr Robertson missed me so much  he was dreaming about me. But it is all
right, I was here.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It was a nightmare.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: He says it was a nightmare b ecause he is worried that I
will come for him one day. Having said that, it might just happen.
18260 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
When this Government was elected in 2008,  we picked up a mess that Labour left
us—Labour and its leftist friends. They left  us a 50 percent increase in Government
spending in their last 5 years, high interest rates nearing 11 percent—

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It was 11 percent, Mr Ross—11 percent. The cost of
living increase was over 5 percent, inflati on of 5 percent, an export sector going
backwards, and a country in recession for the last 4 years. I should also note that it was
a country where crime was getting out of contro l. We had about 70 murders in 1 year as
opposed to the usual 45. It was a country wh ere people did not respect the Government
and they were desperate to get rid of it, and they did, and they gave us the honour of
being able to be their Government.
This Budget is the Budget that brought us back into surplus. We inherited a recession
that had been in place for a whole year be fore we came into Government. It was a
recession that had been in place for a year be fore the rest of the developed world went
into recession. It was a recession where New Zealand led the world into recession under
a Labour Government—a Labour Government. The only thing I would say is thank
goodness it was not the Greens-Labor Government of Tasmania, because there would
have been a recession 5 years before everyone  else. We inherited a decade of deficits—
a decade of deficits. We were told—all the forecasts said—that this country would have
deficits for 10 years. Actually, this year we are out of recession. We are out of deficit.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: And you increased GST, put taxes up—put taxes down for the
wealthy and up for the poor.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: We have also been able to produce a lot more than that,
because balancing a Budget is not just a bout saving money or spending money, Mrs
King. A balanced Budget means actually producing better for our New Zealanders.
In my own justice portfolio I have to sa y that working with the justice sector,
Ministers Chester Borrows and Anne Tolley,  and the Attorney-Gen eral, we have had
the most wonderful time working together to make sure we bring the crime rate down.
The crime rate in New Zealand per 100,000 New Zealanders is now the lowest it has
been in 35 years—that is, since 1978. Some of us can just remember 1978, unlike Ms
Ardern, who was still a twinkle in her daddy’s eye. In that time, what we have been able
to do with the work of the marvellous New Zealand Police, the Department of
Corrections, the Ministry of Justice, and th e courts is bring that crime rate down and
retain that. The last 4 years of the National- led Government have led to a 20 percent cut
in crime, a massive decrease—a massive decrease.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: No, it hasn’t.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Mr Little does not like that, but I am sorry, that is true.
In addition, let us look at ACC. My collea gue the Hon Nick Smith inherited an utter
mess from Maryan Street. What a useless Minister for ACC she was. She was only
slightly better than the other useless Mini ster, the Hon Ruth Dyson. Having said that,
we had to deal with the levies  and, in fact, this year and fo r the last few years we have
been able to drop the levy rates. We are now in the position of being able to tell Kiwis
that after a decade of Labour  running down ACC and rem oving any confidence in the
system, we have been able to retain it. We are able to say that, actually, ACC is now one
of the most competitive services in the wo rld, compared with anything even remotely
comparable with that. What we have been able to do is say that we can deliver sustained
levy cuts. There is no point delivering a cu t one year and then putting the levy up the
next year—absolutely hopeless.
In this Budget we have also been able to say something for transport. I want to deal
with transport for this reason. This G overnment is delivering $200 million for the
southern corridor. For those of you who are not intently interested in the southern
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18261
corridor like I am, that is the southern motorway. So that is really from Hill Road in my
electorate down through to Drury in my electorate. I have to say, it is a marvellous thing
that we will be widening that southern mo torway. That will save people so much in
terms of money and time. It will save the envi ronment. It will save so much in terms of
productivity. That will be one of the biggest  differences for people in the southern
region of Auckland and also for those travelling from Hamilton—those who have to use
that area. That is one of the biggest things that I am most proud of in this Budget.
I am not quite as proud of that as I am of  what the Hon Tony Ryall has been able to
produce in health, I have to sa y, particularly the free genera l practitioner visits and free
prescriptions for all children under 13. In my opinion that is th e standout result of this
Budget. It is a fantastic result for New Zealand families all over the country. I know that
in my electorate of Papakura, people are so excited by that, so thank you, Tony Ryall.
What we have been able to do is to do much better than just spending money. Where
we have been able to, we have used the money more efficiently. We have also been able
to ask professionals who are involved in these areas how th ey would spend the money.
They have come up with all sorts of ideas. If  you look at the rheumatic fever work that
Tony Ryall has done, that is th e sort of thing where—in many parts of my electorate
there are decile 1, 2, and 3 schools; not all of them, but many of them. One of the things
that teachers say to me is making a huge di fference for children is the fact that this
Government has put social workers in all of t hose low-decile schools. That is the sort of
thing that I think this Government can be immensely proud of. We have not been able to
do it just by ourselves. We work with our support parties: the M āori Party, United
Future, and the ACT Party. I would like to ackno wledge the help they have given us to
be able to bring this about.
Unfortunately, when I look at some of what  has happened over the last few years, I
would ask what it is that the Opposition has,  in fact, supported. Well, actually, not a lot.
Did it, in fact, support  any savings that this Government  could make to get the country
back into surplus in any of the previous five Budgets? The answer  is no, not one. Did
Labour, for instance, support the welfare reform  that has seen so many New Zealanders
get themselves back into work and get a sense of actual independence? No is the
answer. Did Labour ever support tax changes to reduce tax rates paid by every single
New Zealander across this country? The answer is no. Did Labour support 90-day
probationary periods, which were so good fo r small businesses, to get people some
confidence to get back into work, and for sm all-business owners to have the confidence
to give people a chance, to give people an opportunity? The answer is no, it did not care.
Did Labour support Resource Management Act reforms so that people can build their
houses faster and support the growth of busin esses? Well, the answer is no. Did Labour
support housing accords so that we could have  special housing areas? They are in my
electorate, by the way, as well—three of them  now in my electorate of Papakura. Well,
the answer is no. Did Labour support the making of the Hobbit movies in New Zealand
so that 5,000 jobs could be created here ? No. That party’s members are the Hobbit-
haters. The only party members even worse th an them in their record of not supporting
the Government’s moves are the wilted and bitter Greens.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: What a great Budget for New Zealand
families. Up and down the country, people know that the John Key Government is
making children and families a priority in this Budget and is absolutely determined to
back those families. New Zealanders have got every reason to be optimistic about the
future on the basis of this Budget. Through very sound financial management by the
Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, and the rest of the Cabinet, this country is now
in the black and is on a roll. This country is moving forward, and we have options for
how we can invest our finances now that our country is back in th e black. This Budget
18262 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
stands in marked contrast to what you ar e seeing all around the world. Just look across
to Australia, where the health budget has been cut by $10 billion.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: $10 billion. Australia’s growth projection is not as rosy as
here. Things are much tougher over there,  and the Government is having to make
decisions that could not be made under th e Labor-Greens outfit that ran Australia up
until a year ago. Look at Fran ce, where the socialist Presid ent Hollande is cutting $17
billion out of health expenditure. A socialis t President has cut $17 billion out of health
expenditure. That is part of $90 billion wort h of cuts that have been announced in
France by a socialist President. So all ar ound the world, Governments are still taking
significant expenditure actions, but here in New Zealand, because of the sound financial
management of our Government, we are able to produce a Budget that is in the black.
And it is a Budget for families—a Budget for families and a Budget for investing in the
future of New Zealand. It is marvellous to be  serving as the Minister of Health in the
John Key Government, which is putting $1.8 billion into health over 4 years.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: $1.8 billion. That is made up of new money and savings in
order to make sure that we can expand health  services for New Zealanders and meet the
cost pressures that we face. And let me  just talk about what sound financial
management in the health service can de liver. When I became Minister of Health,
deficits in district health boards were expected to be $200 million. We are now on track
to get that down to $10 million or $20 milli on, because of sound financial management
of our system. We are able to have $90 million going into making general practitioner
visits and prescriptions free for children under the age of 13, from 1 July 2015. That is
400,000 children and their families who are going to expect a benefit from this
investment. It is an important preventive he alth measure, as parents will not have to
think twice about taking their kids to thei r doctors, and it will relieve pressure on our
busy hospital emergency departments. We ar e putting an extra $110 million into hip,
knee, and other elective surgeries to build on the record increase in elective surgery that
we have had under this Government.
We should remember that the previous Labour Government doubled the health
budget but the number of people who got opera tions actually dropped. How does that
work? How do you double the health budget and fewer people get oper ations? It just
does not make sense. We want more New Zealanders to get hip, knee, and other elective
procedures, and that is what this funding will be focused on.
One of the things that has been overlooked in this Budget so far is the Government’s
very smart anti-obesity investment in Healthy Families New Zealand—$40 million over
the next 4 years. It is a complete reform of the way that we address the underlying
causes of poor health in New Zealand. Far too often, resources are spread too thinly in
this public health area. This Healthy Fa milies New Zealand project, working across
900,000 of our population, will be building a dedicated health promotion workforce that
will be engaging with early childhood centr es, schools, sports clubs, eateries, and
caterers, and helping them help their co mmunities at a grassroots level to take
responsibility and take action to improve  the health and well-being of their
communities. And we know it works. It is based on a programme that has worked very
successfully in Victoria. It is going to make a big difference to many New Zealand
families and many communities, such as S outh Auckland, west Auckland, and parts of
the South Island as well.
We are also putting in $33 million for faster cancer treatment. What we are going to
be doing here is addressing one of the majo r concerns we have picked up from cancer
sufferers and their families around New Zeala nd. Being diagnosed with cancer is a time
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18263
of extreme anxiety for anybody. There are a lot of concerns about what the future may
hold. This investment is going to allow us to  put dedicated specialist psychologists into
each of the six cancer centres around New Z ealand to help support cancer sufferers and
their families. It will also allow us to ha ve dedicated counselling and social support
staff—up to 20 of these support workers—throughout the country to ensure that patients
who are diagnosed with cancer and their fa milies receive more support and counselling.
We have more than 20,000 New Zealanders di agnosed with cancer ev ery year, and this
is a very important part of how we support those families in their cancer journey. I think
that is a top spend by our Government, including extr a investment for breast and
cervical cancer screening programmes to ensure that more New Zealand women receive
high-quality screening services. In fact, we  now have digital mammography services
throughout New Zealand. That is  providing a much better quality of services for New
Zealand women.
We are making a huge investment also in th e training of our medical workforce. An
extra 38 medical students will be able to go into our medical schools this year, and we
are funding $18 million to provide more postgraduate training opportunities for the
extra graduates who are coming out of medi cal schools. We are gr owing more of our
own doctors here in New Zeala nd, and it is a great investme nt that our Government has
made.
We have got one major cut in health that Labour never crit icises, and that is the cut
of 1,000 managers and administrators. We  have taken out 1,000 managers and
administrators from the health service and we have used that money to back the
investment that we have made in well over 1,000 extra doctors and over 3,000 extra
nurses at the bedsides of Ne w Zealand patients in our hospitals. There are over 1,000
extra doctors and over 3,000 extra nurses at th e bedsides of our public hospitals. It is a
huge investment that is allowing us to pr ovide more elective surgery faster, better
cancer treatment, and more elective su rgery—40,000 more operations, like hip, knee,
and other elective operations.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: There were 40,000 in the last year, compared with what we
inherited under the previous Government.
I have got to say that one thing we have found about this Budget is that Annette King
and Russel Norman do not know how to read a Budget. We have got the Greens going
around the country saying that we  are cutting the health bu dget over the next 3 years.
That is completely wrong. What Russel Norm an has not taken into account is the fact
that the numbers he is looking at do not take into account the extra money that will
come in next year’s Budget and the next ye ar’s Budget and the next year’s Budget. So
he is going around the country trying to tell  people that we are reducing the health
budget. We are increasing it year on year on year. When we started this job, it was much
lower than where we are now. We are building on Budget 2013 with $1.56 billion worth
of health investment this year. But it is not  just about the money; it has got to be about
the results for patients. I make no apology for the fact that this Government has put a lot
of pressure on the public health service to deliver more, and we have delivered more
care for patients. We do not send women to Australia for their breast cancer radiation
treatment, which that party did and made excu ses for. We are treating them all here in
New Zealand faster than that crowd ever  did. We are providing more hip, knee, and
other elective procedures than that party opposite ever did. We are delivering the results
that make a difference, to make this the best country to be young and to grow old in.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speake r. This is a split call
between me and my colleague Holly Walker. I was disappointed last week to be in the
House on Thursday and Friday to speak on th e first bill that the Government passed
18264 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
under urgency. I was disappointed because, although we voted for the bill to extend the
parental tax credit to the pa rents of newborns to 10 weeks and raise it from $150 to
$220, and to extend paid parental leave a b it, it was a bill that did not go any way
towards addressing the poverty of the babies born to our poorest families. It is estimated
that about 15,000 families and th eir babies will be discrimi nated against in the coming
year with this tax credit. Although the extensi on to paid parental leave is a step—a little
step—in the right direction, the Child Povert y Action Group’s Susan St John says that
the $64 million per year that it will cost would have been better spent on giving those
families whom this Government has ignored—t he sole parents, the students, those on
ACC, those people on the very lowest incomes—the parental tax credit.
The latest census information highlights th at the gap between the very wealthy and
the very poor continues to grow in this country. The deprivation index shows the
differences in incomes in all the meshblocks in New Zealand. In Ōtara north the median
income decreased between 2006 and 2013 by 17 .8 percent. Meanwhile, in the nearby
suburb of St Heliers the median income gr ew by 25 percent over the same period. We
all pay the price for inequality. The rese arch shows that adu lts suffering serious
financial hardship are nine times more likely to experi ence psychological distress and
six times more likely to have experienced an unmet need for a general practitioner in the
past 12 months. They are more likely to sm oke and suffer from a range of diseases,
including obesity and obesity -related diseases like type 2 diabetes, and rates of
childhood obesity in deprived areas are 19 percent compared with 3 percent for those in
the least deprived areas. Although the introduction of the free general practitioners visits
for children under the age of 13 is great, some  families cannot even afford the bus fare
to get to the doctor. That is why the Greens have a policy and a suit e of initiatives that
we would like to introduce th at would bring health care to the primary schools to where
those kids are and save those families from more expense.
We see this Budget as a missed opportunity. We could take an investment approach
to our people. One of the best ways to do that is to ensure that there are decent jobs for
people and decent wages so that people can live on what they earn. But what we see are
no measures to do that. In f act, the Government’s own forecast suggests a real wage
growth of only 0.8 percent, and its forecas t for GDP is 2.8 percent, which means that
wages will continue to fall behind, and there is no plan for a fairer sharing of that
wealth. Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to increase, and last year 46 percent of
wage earners did not get a pay increase to keep up.
When we look at the appropriations it is clear  that with a bit of political will we
could make real, meaningful changes that would benefit our lowe st paid. Take the
parliamentary cleaners, for example. They earn less than $15 an hour, and it would take
a measly $210,000 per year for all 30 of them to earn a living wage of $18.80 per hour.
If you compare that with the budget for MPs’  IT and the $7 million for maintenance,
you can see that we are looking at buildings and not at peop le. We believe that we can
do better. We believe in a fair future where people can have good lives, and with that
we need a smart Green economy that works for everyone. Thank you.
Debate interrupted.
