items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I want to use my 5 minutes in this Budget debate to
talk about the arts. From a quick Hansard search of the debate so  far, I think I might be
the only person in the whole debate to have done that so far.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Oh, you wait, Holly.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I am pleased to see that the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage is here.
This Budget allocates $282 million to arts, culture, and heritage. To put this in
context this represents 0.33 percent of total spending in the Budget and 0.12 percent of
GDP. It gives a sense, perhaps,  of the value of the arts to  this Government. The biggest
and, indeed, the only increase in the Budget for arts, culture, and heri tage is associated
with marking the 100th anniversary of the Gallipoli landings next year—$3.6 million for
the National War Memorial and $700,000 for commonwealth war graves. It is
absolutely right that we mark this annive rsary appropriately. That  complex chapter in
our history needs to be appropriately rec ognised, and we need to have meaningful
national conversations about what these events mean 100 years on. We saw some of this
begin to happen on Anzac Day this year. So you will find no argument from the Greens
against the inclusion of that extra funding to  mark this important centenary. However,
funding the commemoration of Gallipoli is not  the same as funding the arts. If we
remove those items related to World War I commemorations from the Budget, the
spending on arts, culture, and heritage has actually fallen by 1.5 percent in Budget 2014.
This is not, as the Minister asserted a year ago, a golden age for the arts in New
Zealand—far from it. I recently conducted an  online survey of people working in the
arts, culture, and heritage sector, because I wanted to know directly from those working
in the area what the major issues facing the sector and facing them were. I was delighted
and slightly overwhelmed to  receive over 1,200 responses, most of which contained
substantive policy suggestions and constructiv e engagement and ideas for fostering the
arts in New Zealand. It seems that the creative sector was very keen to be heard, and not
one person who filled in my survey said it was a golden age for the arts.
What they did say could be grouped into three clear themes.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Name them.

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: I will. The first was resources. Artists are very—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: No, the people—

items.speaker: HOLLY WALKER
items.text: There were 1,200 of them, Minist er. It would take the rest of
my call to list them all.
The first theme was resources. Artists are very worried about funding for their work.
They feel that there are in sufficient funds to go around and that the process of cobbling
together funding from multiple sources can be time-consuming, confusing, stressful,
and demoralising. The second theme was recogn ition. Artists feel that the arts are not
adequately recognised both as a vital part of our economy and for th eir intrinsic social,
18266 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
cultural, and democratic benefit to the public . Choosing the arts as a vocation is not a
well-respected career path in New Zealand. Desp ite the fact that we all benefit from the
fact that some people make that difficult choi ce, it is not reflected  in their experience,
particularly when trying to deal with Work  and Income. To have your choice of career
respected whilst accessing the financial support needed is very difficult for people in
this sector.
The final theme was reach. Artists said that as well as funding and promoting the arts
themselves, effort needs to go into build ing audiences and customers for their work,
because there is no point in making creative work that disappears off into a void.
Fostering participation and appreciation of th e arts is just as important as fostering
creative work itself. So those are the thre e Rs. We could add another one as well—the
regions—because another strong theme that em erged was that outside the main centres
artists found it very difficult to forge a car eer in the arts or get recognition for their
work.
I was keen to see whether an y of these things would be  reflected in the Budget.
Unsurprisingly, I am sad to say, they were not. There were no new re sources, as I have
said. It was actually a fall in funding for the arts, if you take out the Gallipoli
commemorations. There was no recognition. Not one person, certainly not the Minister,
has put out a press release about what the Budget does for arts and culture. And there
was nothing to assist artists to reach new ar eas. In fact, there was less funding in that
area due to the funnelling of funds into the new Screen Production Incentive Grant in
the previous financial year. Finally, for the regions—well, we saved the worst for last.
Not only does the Budget contain nothing to foster community arts in provincial and
regional New Zealand but it slashes funding fo r regional museums by 25 percent. That
is a quarter less funding for regional museums, just like that.
The Government’s attitude towards the arts was best revealed in the now infamous
comment by the Prime Minister, John Key, in a written endorsement to the New

items.speaker: Zealand Literary Heritage Trail
items.text: “While our literary heroes may never challenge the
glory and respect given to our All Blacks, we still need role  models to inspire us.” I
have news for the Prime Minister: our litera ry heroes, indeed all our creative heroes,
already challenge the All Blacks, but they will not do more of it with the help of this
Budget.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The resounding sense that I
am left with in the week after the read ing of Bill English’s sixth Budget is the
extraordinary contrast that it represents. It  represents a contrast between a party and a
Government that are, first of all, united, that are effective, and that are a team that is 100
percent behind their leader, a nd the Opposition benches. It c ontrasts a party that is 100
percent focused on the things that actually matter to New Zealanders and to their
families with parties that—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to
interrupt the honourable member. Can I just advise the House that members who do not
have the floor do not have the right to inte rject on each other while another member is
addressing the House. Courtesy is contagious, members.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: As I was saying, the Budge t contrasts a party and a
Government that is 100 percent focused on the things that actually matter to New
Zealanders and their families with a party th at is content to spend its time focused on
trivia, on scaremongering, and on c onspiracy theories. It cont rasts that with a country
that is back in black after the terrible years of the global financial crisis, the terrible
economic legacy that we were left by the previous Government, and, of course, the
difficulties of the Christchurch and Canterbury earthquakes. It is a country that is back
in black after picking up the 2009 Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, in which
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18267
Treasury said that thanks to  9 years of Labour we were  facing never-ending deficits.
Treasury never believed, when we took office,  that New Zealand would ever get back
into surplus—ever.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: You’re just making it up.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Read the pre-election update. Tr easury said that we were
facing never-ending deficits thanks to th e Labour Government and its 9 years of
economic mismanagement. But what we have is  a country that is ba ck in black, and we
are back in black, in contrast to what we ar e seeing in Australia. As our Prime Minister
has said on many occasions, if you want to know what a Labour-Greens Government
would do to your economy, would do to your population, would do to  jobs, and would
do to families, it is called Australia, whic h is now facing ballooning Budget deficits and
critical slashing of public expenditure. By contrast, we are a Government that every
year, year on year, has put more money into education and into health, and has seen far
better results.
This is Bill English’s sixth Budget, and did he not do a tremendous job? This Budget
is a contrast to the wish list of Labour’s a lternative Budget. It is a contrast to the
unspecified, uncosted waffle that we see fr om the Opposition. If it had anything serious
to offer to New Zealanders by way of contra st, it would have told us. But, no, it would
far rather spend its time slinging mud down in the gutter with the rats. You have to
wonder when the Opposition parties are going to learn. When are they going to learn
that, actually, the measure of  a Government’s success is not how good it is at taking
money off New Zealanders and spraying it around? If that was the measure of success,
if we judged our Governments by how much money they pulled out of the pockets of
New Zealanders and threw around, then, no doubt, Labour would be the party we would
want. If that is your test of success—who takes the most money out of your pocket and
who can spend the most—then you would go to Labour.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why did you delay the ACC cuts by a year?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Actually, the reason the polls ar e telling the story that they
are—Mr Little, for all your shouting—is because what actually matters is the results
you get for New Zealanders. When New Zealan ders come and talk to me, they do not
talk to me about what the non-departmental  appropriation in the Police spend is. They
ask me: “Are we safe on the streets? Will my kids get a good education? Can I get a
new hip or a new knee when I need it? Will my  kids get a job?”. Those are the things
that they talk to me about. On every single one of those, this Government and everyone
in it can stand proudly and say “Thanks to 6 years of prudent economic management,
absolutely, your children have a much bett er chance now of getting a job. Absolutely,
you have a far better chance of getting a new hip or a new knee if you need it.
Absolutely, your children are going to be in a much better position of getting the world-
leading education that all five out of five  of our students deserve. Absolutely, you are
safer on the streets.” That is what matters to New Zealanders, and, even in these tough
times, that is exactly what we have delivered.
One of the most important things I think we have done and that you are now really
starting to see pay off is setting what we call the Better Public Services targets, where,
for the first time, we said to our public sector agencies that what we actually really care
about and what we are going to measure you on is whethe r you are making a difference
in the things that matter. We have said to the health sector that what we want to know is
whether people are getting elective surgery sooner, whether they are getting cancer
treatment in New Zealand, and whether they  are getting breast cancer treatment and
rheumatic fever treatment. Are your childre n getting access to the e ducation that they
need, are there good reporting standards for pa rents, and are more children getting into
early childhood education places? And they are. We have said to the police that we want
18268 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
to know whether New Zealanders are safer. That is what we ar e going to judge you on
as an agency. They have responded stupendously well. That is actually what matters.
Any party that stands up and says “We can do better because we would spend more
money.” misses the point entirely. People car e about whether we are delivering better
results. We can stand here 6 years in a nd say: “We have absolutely better health,
absolutely the safest streets for 33 years, absolutely better edu cation, and absolutely
more chance of getting a job.” That is wh at New Zealanders care about. This year’s
Budget now shows a record of more than $15 billion going into our health sector. As
Minister Ryall has just said, it is not about the number, but what it shows you is that we
are also getting 40,000 more hip,  knee, and other elective su rgeries every year. Forty
thousand people a year are gett ing the surgeries that they need but were going to be
denied under the Labour-Greens Opposition.
I want to talk for a minute about Canterbury, the area that I am from. I want to reflect
on the fact that Gerry Brownlee is doing a tr emendous job in what has to be one of the
hardest portfolios in our Government. For a period of time I was lucky enough to act as
his associate. I have now passed that res ponsibility to Nicky Wa gner, and I know she
will do a tremendous job. But let us look at  Canterbury. This Budget puts another $50
million into helping the Canterbury recover y. That takes our total to $15.4 billion of
support for Cantabrians. We are standing behi nd our second-largest city. We promised
we would, and we are. I want to take a mome nt to look at some of  the statistics out of
Canterbury. As of now, we are looking at 53,500 houses fully completed under the
Earthquake Commission progr amme. Another 47,000 emergency repairs have been
completed. We are currently  seeing 90 homes a day co mpleted under the Earthquake
Commission programme—90 homes a day. In f act, the Government is spending $9
million every day on rebuild receipts in Canterbury—$9 million a day.
Let me talk for a moment about the environment, because this Budget continues this
Government’s real commitment to making sure we actually get results in the
environment—not talk, not rhet oric, not running us down in the international media for
political points, but actual re sults. This is a Government that is delivering the most
rigorous national system of freshwater management the country will ever have seen. We
were committed to that from day one of  coming into Government, and all the way
through it has been a core part  of our programme. This y ear’s Budget commits another
$20 million of new funding to making sure that  that water programme is delivered and
supported. If there is one thing that we have learnt through this proc ess, it is that you
have got to have good information underpin ning good community processes if you are
going to get good, resilient results.
What we have seen from other previous Governments that like to talk about the
environment was that they talked a big game, but did nothing—nada, zero. Were there
ever any mandatory requirements on council s to lift water quality? Not one. Was there
ever a study of what the allocation picture was in New Zealand? Not one. Did they even
ask the question of what water was co ming out of our water bodies and what
contaminants were in them? N o, of course they did not. Th ey just sat back and said:
“That’s a council issue, but isn’ t it terrible?”. This Governme nt is delivering. It has put
another $20 million in in this Budget alone. This is a Government that is going to see
real environmental achievements thanks to  the support of John Key, the National-led
team, and Bill English’s sixth Budget. We ar e back in black, and that means that New
Zealanders have choices and the opportunity to get ahead, and that is why they are
continuing to support the John Key - led Government.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Andrew Little—an opportunity to make a contribution.
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18269

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. It is an
opportunity that I relish and seek to serve the good people of New Plymouth and
Taranaki well in. I want to st art by saying this: there is not hing greater in this country
than National Party members’ capacity for self-delusion. They have come here, day
after day, since last Thursday, spinning a yarn that even they know to be totally untrue.
They talk about the state of the economy. Th ey forget that the la st Labour Government
produced nine surpluses in a row, built up the Cullen fund, built up the ACC fund to
nearly $11 billion over its time, restored the health of that organisation, and delivered
the lowest level of unemployment in the OECD. They forget all that.
They forget Bill English’s own endorsement th at said that because of the state of the
economy, New Zealand was well poised to face the consequences of the global financial
crisis. They forget conveniently that Ne w Zealand suffered a drought in the period
2007-08, which caused the economy to slow down. Apparently, it is the Labour Party of
New Zealand that controls th e weather in this country!  The Labour Party is held
responsible for that. National Party memb ers—all of them who have stood up to
speak—know that they have spoken absolute rubbish about the state of the economy
that they claim to have inhe rited in 2008. The truth is that the last Labour Government
conducted itself and its economic stewardship with aplomb.
The other misleading area that the members of this Government keep talking about is
justice and the crime rate. Well, that balloon was popped some weeks ago at a
symposium organised and hosted by no less a person than the Minist er of Justice. One
of the imported experts from Britain said that  there is nothing that is happening in the
crime statistics that politicians can take re sponsibility for and th at there were other
factors that were dr iving the lower reported crime rate —not the least of which was the
fact that most cars now have security systems, car alarms, and all that sort of stuff.
But here is the other thing. We know that  in this country something else is
happening. That is that the way crimes are managed at the front line is changing. You
talk to any front-line police officer, you talk  to any police prosecuting sergeant, or you
talk to any Crown solicitor, a nd they will tell you that it is not too flash and that the
pressure is on them. The pressure is on them  to reduce the number of charges, to wind
back the charges, to prosecute less, and to try to get that guilty plea for the more
minimal charge. That is what is happening in New Zealand today.
What that means for the victims of crime in  this country is that they are not getting
justice, because the people who are inflicti ng their evil ways upon victims are not being
properly called to account. Soon, at some point in the future, because of the measures of
this Government and the justice sector—it will not be too far away—a person who has a
record of criminal offending that is not prope rly recorded in our crime statistics or on
his or her crime record will appear before a judge on a ba il application, the judge will
have flawed information on which to make a risk assessment and will let the person out,
and that person will reoffend while on bail a nd potentially inflict very serious harm on
an unwitting citizen.
That is how much this Government cares about justice and the victims of crime in
this country. It does not care at all. It does not care at all. You have only to look and see
what is happening with justice spending in  this Budget: $40 million less, and legal aid
slashed—and not just family legal aid, which is what we were told was going to be cut
because the new, magic family law system was going to solve all family disputes in an
instant, but, actually, criminal legal aid is be ing cut back as well. This is not a Budget
for justice; this is a Budget for injustice.
I want to talk about jobs, wages, and the regions. I spend my out-of-Parliament work
time in a region that is claimed by this Government to be loved by it, and a region that it
considers to be very important. But this Government is doing nothing for the regions. It
18270 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
is doing nothing for Taranaki. Its sole achieve ment, after 6 years of being represented
by a National MP in New Plymouth, is to expand a 100-metre bridge, when so much
more is being asked for and demanded by peop le. The expansion of a 100-metre bridge
is all that the people of New Plymouth have  to show for, after 6 years of being
represented by a National MP.
What we see in New Plymouth and Tara naki now is good businesses closing and
jobs going. These are jobs in heavy engineeri ng, the mainstay of the Taranaki economy
for so long—jobs out of Fitzroy Yachts, jobs out of Fitzroy Engineering Group, jobs out
of Tenix, and jobs out of Pace Engineeri ng. That industry is unde r severe pressure
because this Government does not care about the regions. It does not put money into the
regions. It does not care about Taranaki’s roads. It does not care if people in regions like
Taranaki are unemployed and lose their jobs.
While we are talking about unemployment and young people, talking about the
young unemployed, let us talk about the commen ts of the MP for New Plymouth in the
House just the other night when he claimed that things were going gangbusters—he said
that things were going well. Well, the reality is that they are not. Taranaki’s
unemployment rate is higher th an the national average. It was 6.5 percent in March this
year, and jobs are still being lost.
You look at what the Government is not  investing in that  is crying out for
investment. Roading is one of them. Peopl e might make a bit of a joke about me
banging on in this House about State Highwa y 3. It is a crucial arterial road for
Taranaki, and it is totally neglected by this Government—tot ally neglected. The
Government has nothing to say about it, and even less to do about it. The road is crying
out for attention. It is a ro ad on which countless people ha ve died in th e years during
which this Government has been in power , and nothing gets done about the underlying
problems. Nothing gets done about the poor paving, the poor roading, the poor
alignment, the lack of shoulders, or the crumbling cliff faces on the cavernous areas that
the road goes through. This G overnment does not care about it. That is an area that
needs attention.
A Government that cared about  regions like Taranaki woul d not stand aside and just
cheer on what the private sector is doing in the oil and gas industry, as important as that
is. It would know that it has a responsibility  to do things as we ll, to look after the
roading, to look after the port, to look after the other infrastructure in that region, to get
alongside those big infrastructure  businesses like the port, an d others, and to make sure
that the investment is conti nuing, that people are being ke pt in good work, and that the
heavy engineering industry is being supported.
The Government would care about its manuf acturing policy and make sure it had a
manufacturing policy that meant that comple x, sophisticated gear, goods, and structures
could continue to be manufactured here  rather than shutting down our heavy
engineering industry the same way that it is doing with  forestry and sending good jobs
overseas, which is what it is doing. This G overnment’s performance in the regions is
atrocious. This Government’s performance on j obs in the regions is appalling. That is
why this Government is running out of time  and why people in regions like Taranaki
have given up and no longer have confidence in it.
I want to talk quickly about wages. There is one thing th at this Government does not
talk about, because it is guilty of not doing it,  and that is lifting wages in this country.
Last year 46 percent of wage and salary earners—nearly half of the entire New Zealand
workforce—did not get a pay rise, at a time of a growing economy. Oh, the Government
members are very good at standing up and cr owing about 3 percent economic growth.
They are very good at crowing about the fact  that there are more hours being worked
and that earnings have gone up, but ask about  what is happening with people’s wage
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18271
rates and whether people are getting a pay in crease. They have got nothing to say about
it because they do not actually care. They do not actually  care that with a growing
economy, that is the very time people should be getting pay rises. Nearly half the
workforce in New Zealand cannot get pay rises, because our system is busted, broken,
and people cannot get them. Now, in regions like Taranaki, we see not only that those
who cannot get pay rises do not get them  but that good people—the ones who are
getting decent pay rises—are now losing their jobs.
This Government’s record is appalling. Th is Budget has nothing to do for it, nothing
to say about it, and the members opposite, from this Government, should hang their
heads in shame. The Government’s perf ormance is appalling. It has no economic
development plan. It has no regional deve lopment plan. It does not care about the
regions. The regions are suffering. But come September that will change because the
people in the regions know that there are people on this side of the House who care
about the fortunes of the regions, who care about what happens to jobs and families and
good citizens in the regions—regions like Taranaki—and who will be a Government
that will do something about it and lift w ealth, share the wealth, share the national
income, and make this a fairer and more just country.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I want to begin by
paying tribute to Shane Jones. He was an opponent, not an enemy. I very much enjoyed
getting to know him when we both went to Is rael together on a parliamentary exchange
in 2007. He was a great orator, he was a sta unch defender of growth and progress, and
he was a very hard worker. He was what I would say was a great social democrat in the
Peter Fraser tradition, as opposed to those in the Labour Party caucus today who are
lefties in what you could call the Michael Foot or Tony Benn tradition.
Sitting on the left-hand side of Shane yesterday was Hone Harawira, who is,
hopefully, about to accept the torch from Shane to work hard for his people in the north,
but I do not really hold my breath for that. Sh ane really did work extremely hard for the
good folk up in the north, and I want to acknowledge publicly the tremendous assistance
he gave me over my 5½ years as Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations in Te
Hiku o te Ika, and more recently with Ng āpuhi. Hone Harawi ra comes down to
Parliament and gives hellfire and brimstone speeches, but, in contrast to his reputation
as a headline hussy, Shane really got stuck in and wo rked well behind the scenes
because he knew the potential benefits of Tr eaty settlements in the north. I want to say
to his successor, Kelvin Davis, that I wi ll be very happy to work with him in a
bipartisan way to see a settlement with Ngāpuhi.
I say also to Mr Little—one of the few on the other side of the House whom I happen
to respect—that I do think he has absolutely ignored the regional benefit assistance that
comes from Treaty settlements. If you look at  the Taranaki region, for example, and if
you look at the forthcoming settlements with Ngā Ruahine and Te Ātiawa, you have got
almost a couple of hundred million dollars going into the New Plymouth region. That
sort of money is not to be sneezed at. Moreover, iwi are playing a very important role in
housing—for example, Ngāti Whātua’s Weymouth social housing project. An important
aspect of our regional development from a M āori affairs point of view is the work that
we are doing on the reform of the Te Ture Wh enua Maori Act. If we get that right, then
it will be worth billions of dollars to the country. So al l this pro forma Labour Party
research unit nonsense about how we ignore the regions does not stand up to any kind
of scrutiny, regardless of how you look at it.
This Budget has been accurately described as a Budget for families. That is clear
from the extensions to paid parental leave and the increase in the new child tax credit.
The Budget is most important, however, beca use Mr English has kept the home fires
burning—indeed, he has fanned the flames. He has made New Zealand a better place to
18272 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
raise a family again. He is bringing Ne w Zealanders home. Under the previous
administration, a football stadium - full of New Zealanders—over 40,000—were
leaving for Australia every year. Now not onl y are more New Zealanders staying; with
net immigration to Australia only 200 in Ap ril, we are seeing th e return of sons,
daughters, brothers, sisters, and grandchild ren who had never seen their grandparents
before.
This is a Budget that will be welcomed by families, and its benefits are clear—
support for parents, and the reunion of loved ones. I can fully understand why the
Labour Party is not all that happy with it. In fact, the other day in the House, on
Tuesday afternoon, I said to Paula Bennett , my bench mate, that the Labour Party
members seemed very unhappy th at afternoon. She said: “W ell, they’ve just had a
caucus meeting—they’ve had to spend a coup le of hours in one another’s company.” I
think that is the truth of the matter. All ha ppy families are alike; each unhappy family is
unhappy in its own way.
Andrew Little, for example, is very unhappy, because he wants to be Labour’s
candidate in the marginal seat of Rongotai and enjoy my company in the campaign, and,
of course, because he wants to be leader. Under the previous leadership of Phil Goff,
David Shearer, and David Cunliffe, they have all been unhappy. Every time they dump
their old leader and anoint a new one, there is a fresh wave of new tribulation. David
Cunliffe is unhappy because Shane Jones is jumping ship. Phil Goff is unhappy because
he did not jump ship a little while ago. I must say that I am not a psychiatrist, so I do not
understand why Trevor Mallard is always unhappy. Labour used to be unhappy that the
Greens were fringe extremists tarnishing th eir centrist brand; now  Labour is unhappy
that the Greens are about to overtake it as the party of Opposition. Labour used to be
unhappy under Phil Goff and Da vid Shearer. Labour was be ing led by a man under the
thumb of his advisers, afraid to be himself—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. I appreciate that the member has
run out of good things to say about his ow n Government’s Budget, but this is the
Budget debate, and I have not heard in the last 3 minutes—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Look, there have been some
wide-ranging views expressed in the last 14 hours. The Minister is coming to a
conclusion—oh no, he is not—but I invite the Hon Christopher Finlayson to continue.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: David Shearer was a man under the thumb of
his advisers and constantly undermined by Grant Robertson—well, that is the one
constant thing in the Labour Pa rty. But the Labour Party want s me to talk about policy.
I have been talking about Treaty settlements, the reform of Te Ture Whenua Maori Act.
Let us come on to an area that Holly Walk er and I are interested in, because Grant
Robertson was not interested in it as th e Labour spokesperson. It was nice to see
Jeanette Fitzsimons in the gallery this af ternoon. Those were the days when the Green
Party was the nice party. I regret it has descended to be the nasty party, but I have to tell
you that it is also the erroneous party. I want to say—

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: Why do you say that?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Why do I say that? I say that because, for
example, on Budget day Holly Walker tweete d that the regional museums’ funding had
been cut by 25 percent. No, she was wrong. Sh e had simply misread the appropriations
and did not realise that last year’s actual spend included money carried through from the
previous year. The actual a nnual regional museums’ fundi ng is exactly the same. I
called yesterday—I have to tell Holly Walk er—for applications for over $6 million in
funding.
She also tweeted that the heritage funding was down by 23 percent on Budget day—
wrong again. She had misread the appropriations . She did not realise that heritage was
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18273
now in two separate appropria tions, with one dedicated to  the World War I centenary
commemorations, and that the amount had increased overall. World War I
commemorations are among the most important pieces of work that I am working on at
the moment. I know the Greens do not like any kind of recognition along those lines,
but these are important matters, and it is impor tant, I say to Holly Walker, that we look
after this particular period in our country’s history very carefully. I have to say to Holly
Walker that the arts continue to go from stre ngth to strength. It truly is a golden age of
the arts. Te Papa has received further capital spending from the Future Investment Fund,
recognising the national museum and art galle ry, but Holly Walker ignored this. We
have provided $8 million in capital spending this  year, after the neglect of the previous
Clark administration, to deal with important issues of depreciation, and we are working
steadily on the Te Papa North concept, which is going to be fabulous as well.
The National War Memorial Park is being fu lly funded. This is going to be exciting.
The extension is nearly complete, along with the under-grounding, in order to provide a
peaceful and contemplative place and to stop car fumes from polluting Mt Cook School,
as had been envisaged by the previous Gove rnment. I will say to Holly Walker, and she
should listen, that the National War Memorial  Park will also have numerous cycle
paths. I know how important th ey are to the Greens. This  Budget really does have
something for everyone.
This golden age follows on from the successf ul reform of the Ar ts Council recently
and of the Historic Places Trust, and in my outreaching and bipartisan way I
acknowledge the contribution of Catherine Dela hunty there. There is the review of the
orchestral sector, the partnership between  the Government and the Film Archive—
which Holly Walker ignored—and the fiscal  implications of that, New Zealand’s
tremendous guest of honour year at the Frankf urt Book Fair, and the saving of the film
sector from trade union thugs and making it internationally compe titive. There is so
much to talk about in the arts, and that is why I was so disappointed that Holly Walker’s
figures were all wrong. She has ignored the fact  that the arts are do ing very, very well
under this Government. If I have got any advice to offer Holly Walker, for whom I have
enormous affection and respect, may I say that she would be much better off
concentrating on her lobbying le gislation, rather than wasting the time of the House
raising ignorant and incorrect facts about this wonderful area that I am so very proud to
be the Minister of.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Minister of Finance opened this debate by
saying what a privilege it was to deliver his sixth Budget. In response, New Zealanders
will make sure he is unable to deliver a seventh, because his Government’s budgetary
policies are taking us down th e road of traditional macro economic policy: short-sighted
in time, mired in 20 th century ideology, and limited in 21 st century vision. I say this to
the Hon Chris Finlayson, and he should liste n: it is the great-uncle of all Budgets,
cynical in tone, and mercantilist in nature.

items.speaker: The Budget has one laudable component
items.text: it aspires to eliminate the current account
deficit and enter a new era of surplus. That is a necessary aspiration, and the
Government is on target towards a wafer-thin surplus, which it is claiming as the ticket
to electoral victory this year. This nutrien t-thin cake is sugared with the icing of
vanishingly small social handouts to families. This is designed to have the Government
appear as a benign patriarch—a better and br ighter future for all New Zealanders. That
future, according to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, revolves around
growth.
The transparent shortcoming of this election Budget is that it is intrinsically flawed.
It is flawed because it wilfully disregards the difference between sustained growth and a
sustainable economy. The Government cites as its overarching objective the goal of
18274 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
what it calls sustained growth. What could be better than sustained growth? The concept
conjures up a poster image of jobs, health, and education, all in the context of stable
interest and exchange rates and a wizard-like balancing of the books.
Now and again the Minister used the phr ase “sustainable growth” in lieu of
“sustained growth”, without seeming to know the difference. That is a problem because
the concept of sustained growth is flawed. A sustained tr end simply means a continuing
trend. We can have sustained growth. That just means it is aspiring to go on for ever.
We can have sustained growth for a while that is unsustainable—so-called sustained
growth that goes on and on until it breaches the carrying capacity to sustain it.
We cannot have infinite materi al growth on a finite planet . That, in fact, is already
occurring at the global level. The ecologi cal footprint breached Earth’s bioproductive
capacity in the early 1980s. That curve has c ontinued upward ever since. That curve has
continued, with the growth in global popula tion and per capita consumption continuing
remorselessly. It is a new form of sustained growth—sustained but not sustainable.
What does that mean for the national economy, our macroeconomic planning, and
our budgetary judgment for 2014? It means th at when we come to formulate our
priorities, we must begin with the goal of su stainability, rather than sustained growth. It
may be that sustained growth can occur within  the context of sustai nability, but if it
cannot, it must not be the goal.
National’s four priorities in this Budget were identified as responsible management
of public finances, a more productive and competitive economy, delivery of better
public services, and the Christchurch rebuild. By way of contrast, let us consider one
overriding Budget priority—responsible mana gement of the nation’s economy in the
context of global sustainability. Let us cons ider four supporting goals to that. One,
responsible public finances towards a balan ced, net international investment position;
two, higher economic productivity; three, better public services for greater social equity
and higher quality of life, as measured by th e genuine progress indicator; and, four, the
Christchurch rebuild.
Bill English ended his last Budget statement with the comment that “New Zealand is
among the first developed countries to achieve  a return to normal economic settings.”,
but the global economy is on anything but normal economic settings. Bill English may
wish it were, but it is not and never will be again. Until we regard ourselves as
ecological stewards in our budgetary planni ng, until we regard ourselves as being
responsible for sustainability above all else, those economic settings will never again be
normal. That is what is so deeply flawed in this 2014 Budget.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jan Logie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: This Budget delivered a small fiscal surplus, but today I
would like to share with this House some stories from the community on the human cost
of this Government’s decision to prioritise  tax cuts for the wea lthy. This Government
has offered crumbs to some of the poor and has told the newborn babies of beneficiaries
that they are not even allowe d up to the table, let alone a llowed their fair share of the
pie.
Disabled people are amongst the poorest people in New Zealand. Last year the
Government changed the law, to deny equal human rights to family members caring for
them, thereby compounding their family povert y. This year, within the income support
budget, we have seen further cuts specifically  targeting people with disabilities. In 2012
the Government slashed the disabili ty allowance by $37 million—9.2 percent—by
removing funding for some medicines and alternative treatments, cutting funded
services for beneficiaries, and reducing numbe rs getting the allowance. Last year we
saw the disability assistance budget underspe nt by $2 million, and now the Government
is cutting that budget line again by a bit more  than $5 million. This is despite rising
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18275
costs. It costs more to achieve a normal st andard of living if you have a disability. In
fact, research shows that it can cost ove r $2,500 a week more just to have a normal
standard of living if you have a significan t disability. There are obviously other funding
sources for people, but not for everyone, and there are widely acknowledged gaps
between health, ACC, and Work and Income.
Many people whom I have spoken to who have disabilities say they have lost
considerable amounts of money per week from  their benefits over the last couple of
years. There is a general consensus that wh at they receive from Wo rk and Income does
not cover anything like the real costs of living with a disability. To get the disability
allowance you need to provide receipts. But if you cannot afford to cover the cost of the
item in the first place, you cannot claim for it. Further, some things have now been
deemed standard costs and not disability costs,  and they will not be paid for. Disabled
people are now having to regularly visit thei r doctor to verify their disability, which
they then have to pay for, and their doctor’s diagnosis is not uncommonly overridden by
Work and Income staff, “employed experts”, who may have no expertise at all in that
health area.
I have heard from one person who told me  about getting a urinary tract infection
because he is supplied with only four le g bags per annum, when the recommended
minimum is eight. There are other people I have heard from who have developed
infections and pneumonia because they do not  have internal temperature regulation and
they cannot afford to heat their homes properly. I have heard from people who have
disabilities who are significantly underweight  because they can afford only one meal a
day. I have been told by a health practitioner that they had a patient with mental health
problems who was so stressed by the Work a nd Income system that it had induced a
psychotic episode that put them into hospital.  I have been told by more than one person
that they have been told, against the pol icy, that they can claim up to only two
incontinence pads a day. Where is the dignity ? It is clear, from the stories that I am
hearing, that although problem s are not universal, they ar e common enough that, to be
sure, real harm is occurring. These are stories of some Dickensian nightmare.
The Government is reducing budgets in th e face of hardship. Although some Work
and Income staff are doing their best, the reduced funding, lack of expertise, and an
entire goal to reduce the Government’s welf are liability, instead of supporting people in
need, means people are suffering severe indignities. The Government’s line, in response
to these challenges, is usually that the Gr eens would just leave people to rot on the
benefit. This is not true. We would ensure that people can live in dignity, and we would
implement a proactive equal employment opportunities policy, an agenda, to remove the
barriers to employment. We believe that mo st New Zealanders would be happy to pay
for that.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call. I call the Hon Maurice Williamson.

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: It is a split call, and
because it is only 5 minutes my intention is to focus on only one issue, and that is the
issue of Bill English and his six Budgets. Budget 2014 did not just happen; Budget 2014
was the result of 6 long, hard-wor king years to get the country to where it is. It is quite
clear that when we came into office th e world was about to go through the most
catastrophic global financial crisis that it has had ever since the Great Depression.
Members on the other side and members of  the Post Primary Teachers Association
and the teachers union are of ten going on—I actually th ink quite rightly—about how
you cannot judge a teacher just by the results of their classes, because if they happen to
be teaching a decile 10 class with rich parents and lots of resources, it is a lot easier than
if they are teaching a decile 1 class where the kids do not have those resources. I hear
18276 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
about that all the time from the other side. That same comparison works with finance
Ministers. If they are preparing Budgets wh en there are times of  abundance and surplus
and world growth, as Michael Cullen had—no wonder he was able to produce such
surpluses he did not know what to do with them. He had to set up things like the Cullen
fund because the world was just growing.
But New Zealanders know that in 2008 a glob al financial crisis hit the world and
countries much bigger than us, much stronge r than us, took a battering. Go to Europe
and have a look at its big economies that just  had their guts rippe d out from them. My
credit today goes to a finance Minister of a very small economy of only 4 million
people, who took a look at the future and said: “We are going to have to do some
amazing, amazing accounting work to keep our books in balance and to finally get some
surplus.” He said he was not going to do the harsh “Let us put all the pain and suffering
back onto the people of New Zealand.”, so he  took the rough edges off it, he got under
way with his first Budget in 2009, and the sixth Budget in 2014 is a resulting
culmination of that.
But it was not even that easy. He only just  got going into that 6-year cycle when
along came the biggest disaster this count ry has ever had cal led the Canterbury
earthquakes. Billions of dollars of dama ge was done to the economy on top of the
global financial crisis. The good news is—and I say it is really good news—that the vast
bulk of the voting public out there understa nd the circumstances that the National
Government has had to work under to get us to where we are. They understand that the
pain could have been way more severe but Bill English’s prudent fiscal management cut
the rough edges off it. They know when they  look across the Ditch to Australia just
what an appallingly managed economy can look like, and they see the pain and the
suffering that is going on. And now the time has come for them to make a decision
about the future.
I have told this House many times, and I wi ll say it to members again: elections are
not won and lost on 457 different items; they are lost and won on one major split. Is it
“Is the Government tired and clapped out, and is it time for it to go?” or is it “Don’t put
it all at risk, because this lot have done a good job.”? I have been around this place a
long time. I have seen when those “time for a change” tsunamis come. I saw one come
in for Labour in 1990, and no matter what it di d, it got wiped out. Trevor Mallard went,
Phil Goff went, Annette King went—it just  wiped them out. I have been on the
receiving end of one in 1999 under Jenny Shipley. No matter what we did we got wiped
out. But do I detect anything like a “time for a change” move out there? No, I do not. In
fact, there is not even the embryo of a “tim e for a change” move, but there is a huge
concern about the “Don’t put it all at risk.”
Bill English has delivered to this National- led Government the most amazing set of
six Budgets and put us in a spectacularl y good position for the future. The general
public of this country will thank him for many  years to come for being the best ever
Minister of Finance under the worst possible conditions he could have ever experienced.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.role: Minis ter of Pacific Island Affairs
items.text: It is a
pleasure to rise to speak to this Budget debate and, along with my colleague who has
just resumed his seat, the Hon Maurice Williamson, congratulate the Minister of
Finance, Bill English, and our Prime Mini ster on another effective Budget for New
Zealanders. It is a Budget that has family a nd children at its centre. It is a Budget that
leads to a surplus in 2015. And it is a Budget that at its core focuses on th e issues that
really matter to all New Z ealanders, and they are heal th, education, jobs, housing,
economic growth, and, above all, living within our means.
There is $173 million on paid parental leave. That is for supporting children, when
they are at their most vulnerable, and fam ilies during what may be difficult times, and
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18277
we are there to support them. There is the $90 million on free doctors visits and
prescriptions for kids under 13. Over 400,000 ki ds will benefit, and 45,000 of these will
be Pacific. Again, we are there to support them.
The feedback I have been getting in Ma ungakiekie and from Pacific communities is
that this Budget is good for our families and can help with tight family budgets. It
shows that National cares about the vulnerable, it cares about those who are in need, and
it cares about those families who are strugg ling. We know that hea lthy kids are better
able to learn, grow, and develop. That is also why we are inve sting a further $150
million into early childhood education. You see, our children deserve the best start to
life, and this Government is delivering on th at promise. For Pasifika that means the
number of early childhood education centres  has increased by 9 percent to 96 early
childhood education centres across this count ry. The number of children enrolled has
increased 12 percent in the last 5 y ears, and now there are over 3,100 children
participating in early childhood education. The number of teachers for Pacific children
has gone up 30 percent under this National administration, and there are now over 1,900
early childhood teachers across this country.
This Budget is about more jobs. We e xpect another 172,000 j obs by 2018. In only
this last year we have had 84,000 jobs adde d and created in our country and, again,
7,900 of these are for Pacific people. What th at shows is that a job promotes self-
reliance, it promotes independence, and it promotes the abil ity of all New Zealanders to
feed, clothe, and develop and nurture th eir families. Average wages have gone up
$3,000 in the past 2 years, and they are fo recast to increase by another $7,600 by 2018.
For Pacific people the average weekly earnings have gone up  14 percent, or $94, in the
last 5 years. There have been low increases in the cost of living. We know that wages
will have grown by 13.9 percent by 2018, and inflation will grow by only 9.8 percent.
This Budget is about families and our child ren. This Budget is about New Zealand
getting to surplus, and it is about the issues that matter to all New Zealanders.
On 20 September, New Zealanders will have  a decision to make. Will they vote in a
Government that has a record of success and a vision for a great  New Zealand, or will
they vote in a rabid Opposition that is divi ded and devoid of good ideas? I say they will
vote in the National Government again. They trust this National Government to look
after all New Zealanders: those who are vulne rable, those who are in need, and those
who require help. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand that the next call is a
split call—the Hon Damien O’Connor.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : Today the
Parliamentary Library had a promotion of ag ricultural industries. As we walked into
Bellamy’s, I could not help but borrow this ic onic symbol, the sheep, to raise in this
House today. This country was built off th e back of the proud sheep. Wool was worth
the value of gold in the 1950s and is still a core part of one of our biggest industries, the
meat industry. But the sheep, unfortunately, is  not the brightest of animals. Like the
National Party, it has this terrible tendency to follow its leader blindly. When the leader
is an international money trader, it is little wonder that that party fails to come up with
any vision or any long-term plan for the future of the New Zealand economy.
Can I say that this is a Budget of wasted  opportunities, and nowhere is that more
apparent than in the meat industry itself. Can I say that the Budget fails to do anything
to drive down our overvalued New Zealand dolla r. It fails to do anything to curb ever-
increasing interest rates and bank profits , which continue to climb. The Budget
desperately manipulates figures  to come up with a so-called surplus. The social and
economic deficit in this Budget will become apparent over the next few years.
18278 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
From a rural perspective, th e jobs we desperately need are still in many ways linked
to our proud sheep. But, thankfully, we are a little more intelligent than National. What
we are seeing in the sheep industry is that  carcases are now being exported to China.
We see dryland areas being converted into dair y. We see that pasture-fed protein is now
changing to grain-fed protein. That is a lost opportunity because the Minister for
Primary Industries in the Government contin ues to be a sheep instead of becoming the
shepherd. It is about time Minister Guy b ecame the shepherd and gave some guidance
to an industry where thousands of workers up and down this country are fearful of their
jobs because of the declining meat industry.
Communities are at risk. Thousands of M āori workers and thousands of other Kiwis
up and down New Zealand who have kept our c ountry going are now at risk because of
the declining industry and the fact that th at Government did nothing. The Government
threw money at the meat industry; it offered no guidance. Its Primary Growth
Partnership grant system in the Budget has al located the best part of $350 million to the
meat industry, with little or no accountability. The Audito r-General is investigating that
now, and I look forward to the outcome of th at. The Primary Growth Partnership grants
are an insult to every taxpayer because the Government is giving money to its mates and
pretending that it is going to do something to revive the meat industry and give security
to those workers up and down this country.
This country desperately needs a Labour  Government with vision, a Labour
Government—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Ha, ha!
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: Mr Henare would do well to go and read not Labour
Party propaganda or wisdom but the New Zealand Farmers  Weekly of this week.
Labour’s monetary policy is sound. Until we sort out our monetary policy, no export
industry can have security, a nd no export industry can invest  in the way it needs to and
know that it will get a fair return. If  I can quote from the wisdom of the New Zealand
Farmers Weekly, it said that the dollar “is 5-15% higher than is justified by the
country’s earning potential.” and is costing us $9 billion a year in export earnings. That
would pay off a lot of this de bt of $56 billion. In summar y, can I quote th at “Labour’s
plan is not perfect.”—we do not claim that—“But it should reduce dependence on
foreign lenders and their expensive money and push the currency down to more export-
friendly levels. And for that, it deserves fa rmers’ backing.” The reason the National
Government will not intervene is because it is led by a money trader, and that
Government, like this thing here, is a bunch of sheep and will take this country down
the gurgler unless we change the Government and put Labour in power.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Nanaia Mahuta—5
minutes.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: National’s Budget 2014
is more rhetoric than reality. The very ri ch are getting richer and the very poor are
finding it much harder. I am from a little town called Ngāruawāhia—many of you might
know it—and we just tell it how it is. Many of us in this House have heard stories from
nurses, from teachers, from social workers,  from road workers, from subbies, from
people at the checkouts. They are asking w hy they are working harder for longer for
less. They know, actually, that  the National Government ha s not provided the brighter
future that it promised.
On 20 September 2014 people will be turn ing out to hold this Government
accountable. This Budget has not delivered to them. In fact, people are sitting at home
listening to this debate and saying that actually it is easy to  balance the books when you
sell off State assets. It is easy to balance the books when you sell off State assets, but
what have we got to show for it?
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18279
I want to highlight several things about this Budget. Th ere is no long-term plan for
New Zealanders that will deliver  a brighter future that is more sustainable, delivering
better jobs for higher wages. This Budget does not address the se rious challenges of
inequality and poverty that families across th e country are feeling in very real ways.
This Budget does not leverage to wards opportunities where the M āori economy can
make a significant contribution. Where the rubber hits the road  and where normal
people at home judge whether or not this Budget is successful is on the issue of jobs.
Let us look around. In our regions there have  been a number of job losses, which do
not just affect individuals; they affect wh ānau. In places like Northland, the Bay of
Plenty, Gisborne, and Manawatū, look at the statistics. They tell a very different story to
the one that the Government is trying to have you believe . The regions are suffering.
There have not been solutions to grow more  jobs in those places where families really
need the opportunities. They need to be backed.
In the area of our kids, yes the Budget did provide for free health care for under-13-
year-olds, but that is only if you can access those services. Go to places along the East
Coast in Meka Whaitiri’s electorate, Ikaroa-R āwhiti, and you actually have to get to the
place where the doctor is to be able to acc ess those free health care services. Go to
Kāwhia—people will tell you the same thing. Go to Manurewa, where the doctors are
already oversubscribed from d ealing with a number of vulne rable users, and they will
tell you they are already under pressure. Will this funding deliver extra doctors in our
clinics? Can the Government answer that? If  you are going to provi de free health care
for under-13-year-olds where it ma tters, then it has to be about delivering into areas
where there are high needs and vulnerability and to those communities where there are a
number of factors that limit access to free health care.
In the area of homes, what we see is a solution from the Government where it is
transferring the responsibility for social housing to the third s ector. It is transferring the
responsibility for social housing to the thir d sector and stepping back and away from
that responsibility. To me, that does not sound like upholding the opportunity for people
to have affordable rentals; that is passing on the problem. And that is what is happening
here under this Government and its Budget. In  fact, what is also happening in the space
of housing is that homeowner ship is a distant prospect  for low and middle income
earners who are scrimping and saving to try to get a 5 percent de posit, let alone a 10
percent deposit. It is a very real challenge.
If this Government is going to stand up and promote a Budget that is delivering on
the fronts of jobs, kids, and homes, on all th ree counts it has failed miserably. There are
serious challenges. You cannot just put a plaster on a wound that is beginning to fester.
That wound is inequality and poverty. This Government will be judged on 20
September by the way in which it helps the most vulnerable in our society. Alongside
my colleagues in the Labour team, I say that they have failed miserably.
Finally, on the issue of Treaty settlements can  I say that if this was a Budget that
delivered opportunity to leverage off Treat y settlements, we would see far different
solutions than the ones coming from the Government. The Government is rushing
through Treaty settlements. There will be aspect s that will come back to challenge this
Government and make it accountable for what it is doing in this space. The Budget has
failed those most in need abysmally, and the Government will be held to account.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is a great privile ge to stand and take
a call in this Budget debate today. We in this National-le d Government are very proud
of our 2014-15 Budget. We are very proud of its family focus, including $500 million of
support for New Zealand families, which ha s found favour with New Zealanders right
across the country. In my ow n electorate of East Coast, which has many families
struggling to make ends meet and too many communities with very high social
18280 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
deprivation, the free doctors visits for children up to the age of 13 have been welcomed.
I would say that they have been extremely welcomed, and I have had numerous phone
calls into my office. Also as an area where many women are working one, two, or, in
some cases, three seasonal jobs, the expansion of the criteria for paid parental leave has
also met a great need as we seek to suppor t newborns and their mums in those early
weeks and months.
We in this National-led Government are ex tremely proud of our Prime Minister and
our Minister of Finance, w ho have steered this country through some of the toughest
economic times ever seen since 1931. We have been very lucky to have the leadership
that we have had from John Key and Bill E nglish. We in this National-led Government
are very proud that we are to be finally back  in surplus, ahead of most of the developed
world, without having to have made the sava ge cuts that we have seen our friends
around the world have to make in countries like the US, the UK, and then, just recently,
our closest neighbour, Australia.
How wise our leaders were to resist th e calls from the Opposition—Labour and the
Greens—to spray millions and millions of dolla rs around to artificially stimulate the
economy to create jobs. They were largely make-work jobs that Opposition members
were talking about. That was what they were  begging us to do at the time. They are not
saying that now, of course. Now they are sayi ng that they would have done the same as
us, that they would have been fiscally respons ible, etc. But, actually, in this House they
opposed every single change that this Govern ment made to try to restrain Government
spending, which had got out of control unde r the previous Labour Government. But,
look, let us face it: the Opposition never lets the facts get in the way of a good story.
This Budget delivers so much to our communities in ways that we know will make a
tremendous difference, like $22 million to budgeting services. What a great job our
budgeting services around the country do. I know that in Gisborne and Whakat āne, as a
result of our welfare reforms, their offices  have been working with more and more
families. They have welcomed the extra reso urces, because that enables them to make
huge changes and differences in the lives of some of New Zealand’s families.
An amount of $33 million will go to help th e most vulnerable in our community, the
children who are at the greatest risk of be ing bashed, of being beaten, and, in some
cases, of being killed. I was delighted that the Minister for Social Development today
announced those extra Children’s Teams. Two of them are coming into my electorate—
one in Gisborne and one in Whakat āne. Both communities have a dreadful record of
vulnerable children being hurt by those who should be taking care of them.
We in this National-led Government are proud that Budget 2014 builds on the hugely
successful results in recent years in reduc ing crime and reducing reoffending, to make
sure that we have fewer victims out in our  communities and that more New Zealanders
can feel safe in their homes, in their communities, and in their workplaces. I want to put
it on record here today that the police and corrections will  continue to target their
resources to where they know they will make the most difference, and they will work
smarter. They will work smarter because that is  what it is all about. It is very clear that
the Opposition does not understand that. It thinks that if you throw more money at
something, it is going to get better results. We  know that that is not the way it works.
We know that we can deliver better public  services by actually working smarter.
Certainly in the justice sector we are seei ng that on a daily basis—working together and
working smarter. The Opposition does not understand that.
Can I say here today that the police’s core operating budge t is being maintained at
$1.46 billion in 2014-15. I know that the Oppos ition has tried to make much of some
expenditure from last year that has not b een carried over into the 2014-15 year and has
described it as cuts. Well, that is just not true. Restructuri ng human resources and
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18281
finance, implementing the Criminal Procedure Act, a road policing underspend, sending
more people off to the Solomons—these are th ings that happen just once, so why on
earth would you carry over the funding for that into another year? I know that it is really
difficult to read Budget figures when you are in Opposition and they are just looking for
a quick headline, but, actually, the facts ar e that the police’s baseline funding has been
maintained. And we have seen over the la st 4 years, as the police budget has been
maintained, that they have worked hard to reduce recorded crime to a 30-year low. We
have seen a reduction in crime of 20 perc ent, and they have done that by working
together and working smarter.
We have heard the Labour Opposition cri ticising the police for that. Opposition
members minimise the effort that the police have put into reducing those crime rates, by
saying that it is happening a ll around the world. Well, I ca n tell you that it is not
happening around the world to the extent that  it is in New Zealand. We are world
leaders. Our police are doing a fantastic job, and they de serve the support of every
member of this House to pat them on the b ack. People out and about tell me that foot
patrols—having more police wa ndering around in the central business district, keeping
an eye on what is happening, and out a nd about in vulnerable neighbourhoods—make
them feel safe and actually st op crime from happening in the first place. This is about
how we work smarter and support our police to deliver safe communities.
Budget 2014 also supports the Prime Minister ’s Better Public Services targets to
reduce reoffending rates by 25 percent by 2017. Corrections are doing a fantastic job.
They have increased drug and alcohol reha bilitation places both for prisoners and for
those who are serving community sentences,  alongside providing much, much greater
access to education and skills training, because  we know that those are the things that
will make a difference to the lives of those pe ople as they finish their sentences and go
back into our communities. Seven and a ha lf thousand prisoners leave prison and go
back into our communities. The Government invested $96 million over 4 years to
increase that rehabilitation, and we now have  9,300 fewer victims of crime a year as a
result of a 12.5 percent reduction in reoffending. That is making an enormous difference
to the lives both of the offenders and of the people in their communities.
We in the National-led Government are proud of our justice sector , and we back it.
We applaud its hard work and its dedication, and we encourage the sector in its desire to
work smarter and to deliver better results and safer communities. We know that cash is
not king, as our colleague Shane Jones talked about last night. Cash is not king. When it
comes to public services, it is the results that count. It is better results for New
Zealanders, and in the justice sector it is better results so th at people can feel safe living
in their communities. I am proud to be part of a National-led Government, standing and
delivering the 2014 Budget.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is a privilege to be able to just wind
up this Budget debate as the Government looks to a confidence vote with some
confidence. I was very pleased to hear Mi nister Tolley’s speech, because she, along
with other Ministers, has done an excellent jo b over the last 6 years now—almost 6
years—of providing better public services when we have had a tight budget, and we
have done it again this y ear. At a time when the Gove rnment is spending less new
money, by a large factor, than the prev ious Labour Government, we are seeing
improvements in those kinds of issues that are at the core  of the purpose of our public
services. This is a Government that seeks to resolve problems and reduce misery, not
fund a system that feeds off it.
That is where the Labour Party is. The Labour Party believes in State monopolies
that fund services that feed off misery. La bour does not want problems solved, because
if you have less misery, you have less Government. That is a key to this Budget.
18282 Budget Debate 22 May 2014
Under this Budget the Government will spend 30 percent of GDP—down from 35
percent just 4 years ago. We have been ab le to control expenditure not by slashing and
burning but by understanding the core drivers of criminal behaviour, of educational
failure, and of social dysfunction, and starting to act on them. I say “starting” because it
is pretty clear that the changes we are bri nging about in public services are only just
getting going and the benefits are only just starting to flow. There is so much more to be
done. That is why we have a surplus. We have a surplus because what works in our
communities works for the Government’s books. Less crime, less spend—you get a
surplus. More educational achievement, less remedial teaching—you get a surplus. That
is what is working. That is in the context of a growing economy.
We are having a confidence vote. This is a confident Budget for a confident
country—a Budget for a country that knows wh ere it is going from a Government that
knows what it is doing. That is why it is going to win the conf idence vote in this
Parliament. It is because it is in the context of an ec onomy that is growing and New
Zealanders beginning to understand that all New Zealanders  can share in the benefits of
that growth. This time around, it is New Z ealand families with young children. That is
the product not of any particular big decision in  this Budget or in the previous five from
the John Key - led National Government; it is  a product of considered and consistent
change over time, always working towards su stained economic growth that can deliver
dividends to New Zealand households year after year. New Zealanders do not really
measure growth in terms of GDP. They meas ure it in terms of better job security—and
it is a lot better now than it has been fo r a long time—and whether their incomes are
likely to rise. If we achieve, if New Zealand achieves—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: You’ve got a pretty bad start so far—46 percent can’t get a pay rise.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is interesting that the member keeps quoting that, because
that is about the average in most years, in cluding when he was in Government. In any
given year when Labour was in Government, 45 percent of the workforce did not get a
pay rise. But I will tell you what they we re doing. I will tell you what was happening.
They were paying interest rates of 10 per cent for first-home mortgages. The cost of
living was going up. Inflation by 2007-08 was 5 percent, and today it is less than 2
percent. So they had no wage rises, inte rest rates were going through the roof to 10
percent, and the cost of living was going up by 5 percent.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What are you doing to lift wages?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: OK, well, let us discuss some of the member’s proposals that
came up in this Budget debate. Here is one. Here is a question: what is the Labour
Party’s immigration policy? All I would sa y is: “Don’t ask Labour because it doesn’t
know.” I think, as Phil Twyford said, it was going to cu t immigration to a net 5,000. So
I expect that this weekend at the ethnic functions in Auckland, Labour members will be
getting up in front of the Indian community  and saying “There’s far too many of you.
We’re going to cut the number. We’re goi ng to slash the number—no more Indians.”
Then, because they are true to their word, they will be going off to the Chinese
celebration and saying “Ah, too many Asians in housing auctions around Auckland.
They’re all Chinese. We’re going to slash th e numbers.” And then they are going to go
down to the Pasifika function. That is right, and they are going to say “No more family
members from the Pacific Islands.” That is  because Phil Twyford and David Cunliffe
said on the radio: “We are going to slash im migration in order to control the housing
market.”

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: That’s what that means.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is not just what it means; it is what they said. It is what
they said. Labour’s immigration policy is to slash migrant inflows. I think it is a bit
weird. I think it is a bit weird from a party th at has traditionally regarded itself as the
22 May 2014 Budget Debate 18283
representative of the migrant communities. But we will be there, Ms Collins will be
there, Sam Lotu-Iiga will be there, Kanwal Bakshi will be there, and they will write
down what Grant Robertson says  to those people. But then it is not weird when you
think about what they are saying to low-income New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: What are they saying?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I will tell you what  they are saying to low-income New
Zealanders. They are saying—I thought you might be interested—“We’ve got this really
bright new idea, which is to increase Ki wiSaver contributions so that the Chinese
buyers don’t have to pay higher interest rate s.” OK? Or: “So that the Indian buyers do
not have to pay higher interest rates.” So  we have asked a simple question: by how
much would you need to increase KiwiSaver c ontributions in a compulsory scheme to
offset a 1 percent increase in interest rates?

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: And what do they say?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: They do not know, so we have done our own calculation and
it is 15 percent—15 percent. So the Labour members in the weekend are going to be out
in the Ōtara market, saying to women who have the second job in a household and are
doing 25 hours’ cleaning in the middle of the night during the week in order to feed
their family: “You have to join compulsory s uper, and we are going to take 9 percent of
your gross income off you. That’s not enough, because when the Chinese drive the
interest rates up, we’re going to put it up to 15 percent.”, and we will be listening. What
a stupid, dangerous, unfair policy. Apparen tly slashing immigration and forcing low-
income people to save money they do not have is Labour’s response to the Budget. I
used to think Labour was lazy, but I did not think it was that silly. I really did not.
I am looking forward to campaigning in S outh Auckland with the growing interest
from the Pasifika vote. We can stand up and say that jobs are growing, wages are rising,
and Labour will stand up and say “We are goin g to slash your take-home pay and make
sure your family cannot come to New Zealand.” But do you know what Labour will do?
It will say something completely different. As  usual, we will have no idea what its
policy is, because in here, in the office buildings, and on Radio New Zealand National it
says compulsory superannuation and slashed migration, but when the members get out
in the suburbs of Auckland, I do not know wh at they will be saying. They will be
sounding like Martin Luther King. That is what they will do—
